false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Assertion hard-codes redundant interpolation count

`expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` encodes the number of times the (now repeated) interpolation happens for a single query: once in `runShardSplitQuery` plus once per shard-group sub-request via `runSplitQuery`. This number has no functional meaning, is coupled to the number of shard groups produced by the mocked label values, and will break on unrelated changes to grouping/shard-size heuristics. Prefer asserting that the interpolated expression reaches `runQuery` (or that it is called at least once per target) instead of an exact call count that documents the redundant interpolation.

New test asserts client-side interpolation of $__auto, which the real code must not do

The test mocks `templateSrv.replace` with a blind string replacement (`input.replace('$__auto', '5m')`) and then asserts that the expression reaching `runQuery` is `count_over_time({a="b"}[5m])`. In the real `LokiDatasource.applyTemplateVariables`, `__auto`/`__interval`/`__interval_ms`/`__range*` are deliberately removed from the scoped vars so that they are interpolated on the backend with the *sub-request's* time range; a frontend interpolation of `$__auto` based on the full range would yield a wrong step/range for each split chunk. The test therefore validates behaviour that neither happens nor should happen in production and gives false confidence; it should instead cover a user-defined variable (e.g. `$step`) and explicitly assert that `$__auto` is left untouched.

Queries are now interpolated twice (runSplitQuery + DataSourceWithBackend.query)

`runSplitQuery` now maps every target through `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)`. The sub-requests built from these targets are executed with `datasource.runQuery(subRequest)`, which calls `super.query()` (DataSourceWithBackend.query), and that method already applies `applyTemplateVariables(q, request.scopedVars, request.filters)` to every target it sends to the backend. As a result each query is interpolated twice: `templateSrv.replace` runs over an already-substituted expression (so a variable whose value itself contains `$something`/`[[something]]` will be expanded a second time) and `addAdHocFilters` is applied a second time to an expression that already contains the ad hoc matchers, which is at best redundant LogQL parsing per sub-request and at worst produces duplicated label matchers in the selector. If interpolation must happen up front for partitioning/step calculation, the second pass should be avoided (e.g. by stripping scopedVars/filters from the sub-request or by only using the interpolated copies for partitioning decisions).

Shard path re-interpolates already sharded expressions

`runShardSplitQuery` interpolates the targets, `splitQueriesByStreamShard` then rewrites them with `interpolateShardingSelector()` (adding `__stream_shard__=~"..."` and `| drop __stream_shard__`) and hands the result to `runSplitQuery`, which (after this PR) interpolates them again, and `datasource.runQuery` interpolates a third time inside `DataSourceWithBackend.query`. So for every shard group the sharded expression is re-parsed and re-processed by `addAdHocFilters`/`templateSrv.replace` twice more. The new test assertion `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` (shardQuerySplitting.test.ts line 112) confirms this: one interpolation became five for a single query. Besides the wasted work, re-applying ad hoc filters and variable substitution to an already-interpolated, shard-annotated expression risks duplicated matchers and double expansion of variable values that contain `$`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
LoggerMiddleware silently loses pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname/traceID when used without the contextual logger middleware

The explicit log params (`pluginId`, `endpoint`, `uname`, `dsName`, `dsUID`, `traceID`) were removed and the middleware now relies entirely on contextual attributes injected by the separate, exported `NewContextualLoggerMiddleware()` plus a registered contextual log provider for the trace ID. There is no compile-time or runtime guarantee of that coupling: `NewLoggerMiddleware` is exported and any stack that omits the contextual logger middleware, or places it after the logger middleware, will produce "Plugin Request Completed" lines with no plugin/datasource/user identification at all — an operationally significant log regression that will not be caught by tests. Also note the trace ID previously came from `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` (unsampled spans included); it now depends on whatever the registered contextual log provider does, so the field can disappear for unsampled traces. Either keep the identifying fields in the middleware or document/enforce the ordering dependency and add a test asserting the fields are present in the final log line.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, so log assertions no longer observe records

`TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()` instead of the receiver. `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` now emits its log line via `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`, so every record is written into a throwaway `TestLogger` that the test holds no reference to. Any test that injects a `plog.TestLogger` into the middleware and then asserts on `InfoLogs.Calls`/`Message`/`Ctx` will see zero calls, meaning the assertions either fail or (if written as "no error") silently stop verifying anything. `FromContext` (and arguably `New`) should return the same instance (or at least share the `Logs` state) so captured logs remain observable.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
Adding FromContext to the exported plugins log.Logger interface is a breaking change

`log.Logger` in `pkg/plugins/log` is an exported interface consumed across the plugin packages (and by downstream/enterprise code). Adding the `FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger` method means every existing implementation outside this repository (or in a repo that vendors it, e.g. grafana-enterprise fakes/wrappers) fails to compile until updated. If the intent is only to let middleware derive a contextual logger, consider a narrower optional interface (type-asserted at the call site) instead of widening the shared interface.

New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no tests

`contextual_logger_middleware.go` is new behaviour that the logger middleware now depends on (it is the only source of `pluginId`, `endpoint`, `dsName`, `dsUID`, `uname` in plugin request logs), yet no test file was added. There is no coverage asserting that the attributes are attached to the context for QueryData/CallResource/CheckHealth/CollectMetrics, nor that downstream logging actually picks them up, so a regression in either this middleware or its position in the stack would go unnoticed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Count-then-insert is not atomic, so the device limit can be exceeded

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` reads the device count with `CountDevices` and then performs the upsert in a separate session. Concurrent anonymous requests (and multiple Grafana instances sharing a DB) can all observe a count below `deviceLimit` and then each insert a new row, so the number of anon devices can exceed the configured limit by the number of concurrent requests. If the limit is meant as a hard cap (e.g. for licensing/billing), this check needs to be done inside a transaction or enforced by a conditional insert.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateDevice reports ErrDeviceLimitReached when the UPDATE matched but changed nothing

`updateDevice` maps `rowsAffected == 0` to `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. On MySQL, `RowsAffected` for an UPDATE returns the number of *changed* rows, not matched rows (unless CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS is set). Since MySQL DATETIME columns have second precision, an existing, known device that re-tags within the same second with the same client IP and user agent produces 0 changed rows and will be wrongly rejected with "device limit reached", denying anonymous access to a device that is already counted. The condition conflates "row not found" with "nothing changed".

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Local cache entry is written before the DB write, letting devices bypass the limit

In `tagDeviceUI` the cache key is stored (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})`) before `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice` is called. Now that `TagDevice` propagates the store error (impl.go:147) and `Anonymous.Authenticate` rejects the request on `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the first request from an over-limit device fails, but the cache entry is already present. Every subsequent request from the same device within the 29-minute cache TTL short-circuits at the cache check and returns nil, so the device is authenticated anonymously and never recorded. The configured device limit is therefore trivially bypassed by retrying the request, and transient DB errors are also "cached" as success.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Device tagging moved onto the synchronous auth path, adding DB round-trips per anonymous request

The previous implementation tagged the device in a background goroutine with its own timeout; now `a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...)` runs inline during authentication. For every cache miss (cache TTL is 29 min, and the cache is per-instance) this executes a `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device WHERE updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ?` plus an upsert before the request can proceed, so anonymous page loads now block on DB latency and the count scan grows with the number of stored devices. On a busy anonymous instance (or after a restart, when the cache is empty) this can noticeably increase request latency and DB load.

New auth.anonymous device_limit setting is undocumented

`cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit` is read from `[auth.anonymous] device_limit`, but the option is not added to `conf/defaults.ini`, `conf/sample.ini`, or the configure-grafana documentation. Operators have no discoverable way to learn the option exists, its default (0 = unlimited), or that reaching the limit blocks new anonymous devices from authenticating.

No test for the main intended behaviour: updating an already-known device when the limit is reached

`TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that a *new* device is rejected once the limit is reached. The core of the feature — that an existing device (one already counted) can still be refreshed via `updateDevice` and does not get `ErrDeviceLimitReached` — is untested, as is the behaviour for a device whose row exists but is older than `anonymousDeviceExpiration`. Given the `rowsAffected == 0` heuristic used in `updateDevice`, regressions here would silently lock out already-counted anonymous users.

Raw error returned from Authenticate yields an opaque 5xx instead of a proper status/message

`Anonymous.Authenticate` returns `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached`, which is a plain `fmt.Errorf` value. Other authn clients return `errutil`-based errors so the HTTP layer can produce a correct status code (e.g. 401/403/429) and a stable messageId. As written, a user hitting the device limit will get a generic internal-error response (and the error will be logged as an unexpected failure) rather than a meaningful "too many anonymous devices" response, making the feature hard to diagnose and inconsistent with the rest of authn.

anonymousDeviceLimit field is typed as `undefined`, not `number | undefined`

`anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` has no type annotation, so TypeScript infers the field type as `undefined`. The backend always sends a numeric `anonymousDeviceLimit` (no `omitempty` on the DTO), and the value is injected via `merge(this, defaults, options)` which bypasses type checking. Consumers reading `config.anonymousDeviceLimit` will see the type `undefined` and cannot compare it to a number without a cast. Declare it as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;` to match `GrafanaConfig`.

args slice is mutated inside the session callback, corrupting the query on retry

Inside `updateDevice` the closure does `args = append([]interface{}{query}, args...)`, mutating the captured outer `args` variable. `WithDbSession` can invoke the callback more than once (e.g. sqlite "database is locked" retries); on a second invocation the query string would be prepended again, producing `Exec(query, query, ...)` and a malformed statement/argument mismatch. Build the exec argument slice as a new local variable instead of reassigning the captured one.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Debug logging left in at Error level, dumping entire ID batches

Six `r.log.Error(...)` calls were added in `CleanAnnotations` (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` (lines 576, 579). These are informational/debug traces, not errors: they fire on every cleanup batch even on full success, and they log the complete `ids` slice, which can contain up to `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` entries (the test in this PR uses 32767). Consequences: log files and alerting pipelines keyed on ERROR level will be spammed every cleanup cycle (now every minute), with multi-hundred-KB lines. Additionally the `"err", err` field in the pre-delete log statements is always nil, since a non-nil error has already returned. These statements should be removed or downgraded to Debug without the full ID dump.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup job interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The background cleanup ticker was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This makes *every* cleanup job (temp file scanning, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, annotation cleanup, user invites, short URLs, query history row-limit enforcement) run 10x more frequently, multiplying DB and filesystem load on all installations. The `clean()` function also uses a 9-minute timeout, so a long-running cleanup cycle now overlaps with ticks that are simply dropped, making the effective schedule unpredictable. Nothing in the PR description justifies this change; it looks like leftover debugging and should be reverted to 10 minutes (or made configurable deliberately).

false_positives.candidate:
New subtest inserts 40003 annotations and 80006 tags, making the suite much slower

The added "should not fail if batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER" case inserts 40003 annotations plus 80006 annotation_tag rows and then deletes 40000 of them, in a test that also runs against MySQL/Postgres in CI. This is a large fixed cost on every run of the integration suite. The parameter-limit behaviour could be exercised with a far smaller dataset (e.g. batch size just above 999 with a few thousand rows), since the threshold in `deleteByIDs` is 999, not 32767.

Per-subtest table cleanup is registered after assertions that can abort the subtest

`t.Cleanup` that deletes rows from `annotation`/`annotation_tag` is registered only after `createTestAnnotations`, `assertAnnotationCount` and `assertAnnotationTagCount` have run. Those helpers use `require`, which aborts the subtest immediately on failure; in that case the cleanup is never registered and the inserted rows persist in the shared `fakeSQL` database, causing all following subtests (which assert absolute row counts and insert explicit primary keys) to fail with cascading, misleading errors. Register the cleanup before inserting the fixtures.

Placeholder-limit workaround keyed on config value and only applied for SQLite

`deleteByIDs` decides whether to inline IDs based on `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` and `GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite`, not on `len(ids)` or on the actual driver's limit. Two problems: (1) for non-SQLite backends there is no guard at all, so an operator who sets `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` above the backend's bind-parameter limit (65535 for PostgreSQL and MySQL's protocol) will get hard failures from the new `DELETE ... IN (?,?,...)` statement, where the previous sub-query-based DELETE used no parameters at all; (2) the condition is driven by configuration rather than the real number of IDs, so the behaviour is inconsistent with the statement actually being built. Consider chunking `ids` into fixed-size groups (e.g. 999/65535) independently of the configured batch size, for all dialects.

Quadratic string concatenation when inlining IDs for SQLite

The SQLite inline-IDs path builds the value list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside the loop, reallocating and copying the whole accumulated string on each of up to `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` iterations. With the 32767 batch size exercised by the new test this copies on the order of gigabytes per batch and allocates tens of thousands of intermediate strings, for every cleanup batch. Use a `strings.Builder` (or `strconv.AppendInt` into a byte slice, as `getAccessControlFilter` already does) instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete puts the wrong logger in the context

`ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` stores the bare writer logger instead of the `log` built one line above with `name`, `kind` and `method` values. Downstream code that pulls the logger out of the context (`klog.FromContext`) loses all request-specific fields, making delete failures much harder to correlate. Every other method in this file passes `log`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine records a storage duration

Inside the background goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, the result is reported with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`. Legacy delete-collection latency/errors are therefore invisible, and the storage histogram is polluted with timings of legacy calls, making mode-3 metrics unusable for detecting broken legacy writes.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records the object name in the `kind` metric label

`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. Object names are unbounded (one per resource instance), so each successful delete creates a new Prometheus label value, causing unbounded metric cardinality growth in the dual-writer histogram and skewing/polluting all dashboards built on the `kind` label. It should pass `options.Kind`.

false_positives.candidate:
"unified store fails" test case only configures the legacy mock

The case named "error when creating object in the unified store fails" sets up the failure via `setupLegacyFn` and leaves `setupStorageFn` nil; it only passes because `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` wrap the same `mock.Mock`, so the legacy expectation also satisfies the storage call. The test therefore does not actually exercise a unified-storage failure and would keep passing if the storage error path regressed. The same pattern appears in the List test case whose name still says "is not implemented" even though List is now implemented.

Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the handler returns

In Create (line 51), Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163) the background goroutine builds its context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming request context. As soon as the handler returns (which happens immediately, because the goroutine is fire-and-forget), net/http cancels the request context, and every context derived from it is cancelled too. The legacy store call will therefore frequently fail with `context canceled` (or never reach the DB at all), silently losing the legacy write that mode 3 exists to keep as a safety copy. The derived context must be detached from the request, e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` before applying the timeout (while still carrying the request's auth/user values).

Create error path records a legacy-store duration for a storage failure

When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`. The failure happened in unified storage, not legacy, so the error is attributed to the wrong store and no storage-error sample is recorded at all. Any alert/dashboard on storage error rate will miss these failures while the legacy error rate shows phantom errors. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

Create passes the caller's object to the legacy store from a goroutine without deep-copying

`d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, ...)` runs concurrently with the request handler while `obj` is the very object the apiserver handler chain passed in; registry stores and legacy stores mutate the passed object (name from generateName, UID, resourceVersion, creationTimestamp). Sharing the pointer with a goroutine while the handler may still read/serialize or further mutate it is a data race (and makes the legacy row depend on timing). The object should be `obj.DeepCopyObject()`ed before handing it to the goroutine.

Fire-and-forget goroutines have no panic recovery and no lifecycle tracking

The four write paths spawn bare goroutines calling into the legacy store. (1) A panic inside a legacy store implementation (e.g. nil map/pointer in the SQL layer) is not recoverable from the goroutine and will take down the whole Grafana process, whereas in the previous synchronous code the apiserver's handler recovery would have converted it to a 500. (2) Nothing tracks in-flight goroutines, so `Destroy()` (line 172) can tear down `d.Legacy`/`d.Storage` while a goroutine is still calling into them, and in-flight legacy writes are silently dropped on shutdown. A `defer recover()` plus a WaitGroup/semaphore drained in `Destroy()` is needed.

Legacy update now reuses the raw objInfo instead of the object written to unified storage

The previous implementation fetched the current object from storage and wrapped `objInfo` in an `updateWrapper` carrying the object actually persisted, so the legacy store received the same final state. The new code calls `d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` with the original `objInfo`, which re-runs `UpdatedObject` against the legacy store's own old object. Consequences: for PATCH/apply requests the patch is re-applied to a possibly different base, and for requests that carry a resourceVersion the value refers to the unified-storage revision, so the legacy update can fail with a conflict. Either way legacy silently diverges from unified storage (the error is only counted in a metric, not even logged). Also note `objInfo` is a request-scoped object being invoked concurrently from the goroutine, which is not guaranteed to be safe for reuse.

No test verifies that the asynchronous legacy write happens

All mode-3 tests only assert the value returned from the unified-storage mock. Because the legacy write now happens in a detached goroutine, nothing in Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection tests waits for or asserts `Legacy.*` was invoked (and `legacyStoreMock`/`storageMock` share one `mock.Mock`, so a legacy call cannot even be distinguished from a storage call). The whole point of mode 3 — that writes eventually reach legacy — is untested, so defects such as the cancelled-context issue in the goroutines cannot be caught by this suite. Use separate mocks for legacy and storage plus a channel/`assert.Eventually` to assert the legacy call.

Update error path records a legacy-store duration for a storage failure

On a failed `d.Storage.Update` the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. The failing call was against unified storage, so storage errors are never recorded and legacy error metrics are inflated with failures that did not occur in legacy. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

go.work.sum changes look accidental and add a duplicate entry

The diff re-adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` even though the identical line already exists immediately above, and adds hashes for unrelated modules (grafana-azure-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, older otel versions) that have nothing to do with the dual writer change. These lines are probably the result of a local `go work sync` with a different module set; they are out of sorted order and the duplicate will be removed again by tooling. Revert the go.work.sum changes unless a dependency actually changed in this PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing re-check of the cache after acquiring the write lock

`GetWebAssets` reads the cache under `RLock`, releases it, and then takes the write lock without re-checking whether another goroutine populated `entryPointAssetsCache` in the meantime (classic double-checked-locking recheck). Consequence: on startup, if N requests arrive concurrently with an empty cache, all N serialize on the write lock and each one re-reads and re-parses `assets-manifest.json` (or performs a CDN HTTP fetch) even though the first one already produced a valid result. In addition, every one of those late writers overwrites the already-published pointer; if a later read fails (file transiently unavailable, CDN error) the code unconditionally executes `entryPointAssetsCache = result` with `result == nil`, discarding a previously valid cached value and making subsequent callers re-do the work / receive `nil`. Adding `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` right after `Lock()`, and only assigning the cache when `err == nil`, fixes both.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing re-check of the cache after acquiring the write lock

`GetWebAssets` reads the cache under `RLock`, releases it, and then takes the write lock without re-checking whether another goroutine populated `entryPointAssetsCache` in the meantime (classic double-checked-locking recheck). Consequence: on startup, if N requests arrive concurrently with an empty cache, all N serialize on the write lock and each one re-reads and re-parses `assets-manifest.json` (or performs a CDN HTTP fetch) even though the first one already produced a valid result. In addition, every one of those late writers overwrites the already-published pointer; if a later read fails (file transiently unavailable, CDN error) the code unconditionally executes `entryPointAssetsCache = result` with `result == nil`, discarding a previously valid cached value and making subsequent callers re-do the work / receive `nil`. Adding `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` right after `Lock()`, and only assigning the cache when `err == nil`, fixes both.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache is overwritten with nil when manifest loading fails

`entryPointAssetsCache = result` is executed unconditionally, including when `err != nil` and `result == nil`. This makes a load failure poison/clear the cache rather than leaving the last known-good assets in place, so every later request repeats the failing file/CDN read and callers get a nil `*dtos.EntryPointAssets`. Guard the assignment with `if err == nil && result != nil`.

No test covering the concurrent access the PR claims to fix

The PR is specifically a data-race fix on the `entryPointAssetsCache` global, but no test was added that exercises `GetWebAssets` from multiple goroutines (e.g. a `t.Parallel`/`sync.WaitGroup` test runnable under `-race`). Without such a test, a future refactor can silently reintroduce the unsynchronized access.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions is dead, self-contradictory logic that ignores the feature flag

`enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`, then returns `false` in both the `if enabled` branch and the fall-through, so the function unconditionally returns `false` and the computed value (and the feature toggle itself) has no effect. The result is a function whose name says "enable" but which can never enable anything, a branch that can never do anything, and a feature-toggle read that is pure noise. If the intent is to hard-disable SQL expressions, this should be an explicit unconditional rejection (with a comment explaining the CVE-2024-9264 context); as written, the next person touching it cannot tell whether the double `return false` is deliberate or a typo, and static-analysis/dead-code linters are likely to flag it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
DuckDB-specific SQL string interpolation of user input left behind in dead code path

`TablesList` still builds `SELECT json_serialize_sql('<rawSQL>')` by string-interpolating the user-supplied query after only a naive `strings.Replace(rawSQL, "'", "''", -1)`, and `tablesFromAST` still parses a DuckDB AST shape (`json_serialize_sql` output, `table_name` keys). This whole path is now dead because `RunCommands` is a stub that returns an error, but it is the exact code shape that led to CVE-2024-9264: if anyone later re-implements `DB.RunCommands`, the injection-prone interpolation is silently re-armed. Since the goal of the PR is to remove DuckDB, this parser (and the unused `DB.TablesList` method added in db.go) should be deleted rather than left as a trap. Note also `tablesFromAST` indexes `ast[0]` without a length check, so it would panic on an empty AST if it ever became reachable.

Error text "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is misleading for users who enabled the toggle

When a SQL expression query is received, the reader now always returns `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`, even for operators who have explicitly enabled the still-existing `sqlExpressions` feature toggle. Those users will see a message implying the feature was never built rather than that it has been disabled for security reasons, which will generate support noise. The message should state that the feature is currently disabled (and the toggle has no effect), and the feature-toggle documentation/registry description should be updated to match, since the toggle is now inert.

No test asserts that SQL expressions are rejected

This change disables SQL expressions in two places (the query reader in reader.go and the stubbed `sql.DB` methods here), but no test is added that asserts a `QueryTypeSQL` query is rejected by `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` or that `NewSQLCommand`/`SQLCommand.Execute` fail. Given this is a fix for a critical RCE/LFI (CVE-2024-9264), a regression test is important: without one, a future change that restores `DB.RunCommands`/`QueryFramesInto` or rewrites `enableSqlExpressions` can silently re-enable the vulnerable path with a green CI. Any existing tests that exercised `sql.TablesList` or SQL expression execution against DuckDB also need to be updated/removed, since they will now hit the "not implemented" stubs.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex-wide lock allows duplicate concurrent builds of the same index

Previously `BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for its whole duration, which made a concurrent `GetIndex` (RLock) block until the build finished, so a second caller observed the finished index instead of starting its own build. Now the lock is only taken around the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write, so two callers (e.g. the startup indexing goroutines in `searchSupport.init` and a watch event going through `getOrCreateIndex`) can both see `GetIndex == nil` for the same NamespacedResource and build in parallel. For file-based indexes this means two goroutines call `bleve.New(dir, ...)` on the same directory (`Root/namespace/resource.group`), and the second one fails (path already exists) or corrupts the on-disk index; for memory indexes the work is duplicated and one index is silently dropped from the cache while documents may still be written to it. The duplicate-build window needs to be guarded per key (e.g. keyed mutex / singleflight) rather than removed entirely.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu

`TotalDocs()` ranges over `b.cache` with no lock, while `BuildIndex` now writes to that map from many concurrent goroutines (the lock was narrowed to just the map write). Concurrent map read + write causes a fatal `concurrent map read and map write` runtime panic. This path is newly exercised on every startup by the added log line in `searchSupport.init` (`s.search.TotalDocs()`), and can also be hit at any time if metrics/logging call it while a watch event triggers a lazy index build. `TotalDocs` should take `cacheMu.RLock()`.

false_positives.candidate:
BuildIndex still discards the span context, breaking the trace fix for builder work

The PR fixes trace propagation in `searchSupport.build` and `GetResourceStats` by assigning the derived context, but `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` still does `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)`. The builder callback invoked at line 126 uses the context captured from `searchSupport.build`, so all storage/list spans produced during the actual index build are siblings of the `BuildIndex` span rather than children, and the BuildIndex span appears empty in traces. Propagate the derived context into `builder(idx)` (e.g. by making the builder accept a ctx or by assigning `ctx, span := ...`).

Context cancel func leaked when Init fails in NewResourceServer

`ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` is created a few lines above, and on the new `s.Init(ctx)` error path the function returns `nil, err` without ever calling `cancel()`. The cancel func is also only reachable through the discarded `server` value, so the derived context (and any timer/goroutine attached to it) is leaked for the lifetime of the process. Call `cancel()` before returning the error (also applies to the `newSearchSupport` error return just above).

Index build now blocks server construction and makes startup fail hard

`NewResourceServer` now runs the full `Init` (lifecycle init + building every namespace's search index) synchronously before returning. Two consequences worth confirming: (1) process/DI startup is blocked for as long as indexing takes (the PR description says it can exceed a gRPC deadline, i.e. potentially minutes on large installs), so nothing else that depends on this constructor — including the HTTP server/readiness endpoint in single-binary mode — comes up during that time; (2) any transient failure during index build (DB hiccup, bleve directory error) now aborts construction and prevents the server from starting at all, whereas before only the failing request errored and a later request would retry `Init`. Consider doing the index build in the background with a readiness gate, or at least bounding it with a timeout and tolerating per-namespace failures.

Postgres integration coverage for the storage-server target is silently disabled

`TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer` now skips whenever `GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres`, leaving only MySQL exercising the storage-server module path. Given this PR changes when unified storage initializes (now inside `NewResourceServer`, i.e. during module startup), postgres is exactly the configuration where a startup regression would go unnoticed. The skip reason ("works locally") suggests the test is actually failing with these changes in CI; the root cause should be understood before merging, and the TODO should reference a tracking issue so the coverage is restored.

Stop()'s initErr is no longer surfaced; requests are served after shutdown

All the per-RPC `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil { return ... }` guards were removed, but `Stop()` still communicates shutdown exclusively by setting `s.initErr = "service is stopping"` / `"service is stopped"`. Since nothing reads `initErr` after construction anymore, calls arriving during or after shutdown no longer fail fast; they proceed against a backend whose lifecycle hooks have been stopped and whose watcher context has been cancelled, producing confusing internal errors instead of a clear "service is stopping" response. Either add an explicit closed/stopped check on the request paths or drop the now-dead initErr mutation in Stop().

init() goroutines write shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` without synchronization

Inside `group.Go(...)` the closures do `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...)`, both of which mutate variables declared in the enclosing function from up to `initWorkers` goroutines running in parallel. This is a data race (detectable by `-race`, and the counter reported in the `namespaces indexed` span event can be wrong/undercounted), and assigning to the shared `err` instead of returning the value through the errgroup can also overwrite an error from another worker. Use a local `err :=` inside the closure (returning it) and an atomic counter.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup registered for the literal alias "alias" instead of the created providers

`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` (lines 381 and 425) registers 21 cleanup tasks against a provider whose alias is the literal string `"alias"`, which never exists. The 21 providers actually created (`idp-alias-0` ... `idp-alias-20`) are therefore never removed, and the cleanup call itself will hit a 404. Depending on whether the realm is re-imported per method this either fails the cleanup phase or leaks providers into other test methods — e.g. `testCacheIDPByOrg` asserts exact counts (6 IDPs for orga) and `testCacheIDPForLogin` asserts 5/5/10, so leftovers make the suite order-dependent and flaky. Use the real alias variable (the same bug exists at line 303 and should be fixed there too).

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login query cache keyed only by realm+mode grows with the number of organizations and is rebuilt per new org

`getForLogin` stores all results for a realm/fetch-mode in a single `IdentityProviderListQuery` whose internal map is keyed by `organizationId`. For `FetchMode.ALL` each per-organization entry contains the full set of realm-level login IDP ids plus that org's ids, so memory is O(#organizations * #realm login IDPs) per realm. Worse, every time a not-yet-cached organization id is seen the code calls `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)` and re-adds a merged query (lines 236-240), i.e. the whole entry for the realm is discarded and rebuilt on the hot login path. In realms with many organizations this means repeated full rebuilds instead of a stable cache. Note also that for `REALM_ONLY` the `organizationId` argument is ignored by the implementation, yet it is still used as the search key, producing redundant duplicate entries for every organization.

Login-cache invalidation decision uses the organization-aware wrapper, so updates can leave stale entries

`update()` obtains `idpById` from `getById()`, which returns the anonymous `IdentityProviderModel` subclass created by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel()`. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` returns false whenever the owning organization (or organizations support for the realm) is disabled, regardless of the IDP's own `enabled` flag. `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate()` then evaluates `getLoginPredicate().test(original)` on this wrapper, so for any org-linked IDP whose organization is currently disabled the predicate is false. If the update also leaves the *new* model ineligible (e.g. only `hideOnLogin` is flipped to true, or `linkOnly` toggled) the method early-returns and no login cache key is invalidated, even though the cached id list (built from a DB query that only filters on the IDP's own attributes) does contain / should now contain that id. After the organization is re-enabled the login lists are served from the stale cache: a `hideOnLogin=true` provider keeps being rendered on the login page, or a newly un-hidden provider stays missing. The comparison should be done against the raw delegate model (e.g. `idpDelegate.getById(...)`) rather than the org-aware wrapper.

No coverage for login-cache invalidation on create/remove of a login-eligible provider

The new test only exercises `create()` and `remove()` with providers that are *not* eligible for login (`hideOnLogin=true` provider created, disabled `idp-alias-1` removed) and asserts the caches survive. The two new `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(...)` call sites in `create()` and `remove()` for an eligible provider are never verified, so a regression where creating or deleting a login-visible IDP fails to invalidate the per-realm login caches (leaving the login page showing a deleted broker, or hiding a new one) would not be caught.

getLoginPredicate no longer matches LoginFilter/getLoginSearchOptions contract

`LoginFilter` is documented as the enum that "contains all fields that are considered when deciding if a provider should be available for login or not", and `getLoginSearchOptions()` is used to build the equivalent DB query. The predicate now additionally requires `organizationId == null || config[kc.org.broker.public] == true`, a condition that is not represented in the enum nor in `getLoginSearchOptions()`. Callers that rely on the two being equivalent filters (query vs. in-memory predicate) will now get different result sets for org-linked providers; the javadoc/enum should be updated or the organization condition expressed as part of the filter set so both paths stay in sync.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default KeyStore provider, not a BC provider

The implementation returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, i.e. typically the JDK SUN provider. BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER is initialized from this method's return value and is then used as the provider name in provider-specific lookups elsewhere in keycloak-core (Signature.getInstance(alg, PROVIDER) etc.). With this provider installed, those lookups resolve against SUN and can fail with NoSuchAlgorithmException for algorithms only offered by BC, which is hard to diagnose. It also instantiates a KeyStore on every call just to read a provider. Returning null (as WildFlyElytronProvider does) or caching an explicit provider reference would be clearer.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead encoder calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER

Lines 114-115 create two ASN1Encoder instances, write rBigInteger/sBigInteger into them and discard the results; the actual DER output is built from freshly created encoders on lines 117-121. These two statements have no effect (only wasted allocations) and are confusing to readers; they should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Malformed ASN.1 input causes unchecked exceptions instead of IOException

readLength() returns -1 for the indefinite-length encoding (0x80) and can return 0. readInteger() then calls read(length) with that value: read(-1) allocates `new byte[-1]` and throws NegativeArraySizeException, and for length 0 `new BigInteger(new byte[0])` throws NumberFormatException. Both are unchecked exceptions escaping methods declared to throw IOException, so an attacker-supplied/corrupted ECDSA signature propagates an unexpected runtime exception to callers of asn1derToConcatenatedRS instead of a handled IOException. Validate length > 0 and reject indefinite-length encodings with an IOException.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

order() is added to the public CryptoProvider SPI interface without a default implementation. Any third-party or downstream implementation of CryptoProvider (including the copies maintained in the keycloak-client repository) will no longer compile and will fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError after upgrading. Adding `default int order() { return 100; }` (or some documented baseline) would keep the SPI backward compatible.

false_positives.candidate:
ES384/ES512 tests use a 256-bit EC key and only round-trip the new code against itself

The key pair is generated with the default EC curve (P-256) and reused for ES384 and ES512, so r/s are always ~32 bytes and the 48/66-byte component paths of integerToBytes/concatenatedRSToASN1DER are never exercised with realistic values. In addition the test only checks that asn1derToConcatenatedRS -> concatenatedRSToASN1DER -> asn1derToConcatenatedRS is self-consistent; it never verifies the produced DER/concatenated bytes against a known-good encoding or against the existing BC-based ECDSACryptoProvider, so an encoding bug that is symmetric in both directions would pass. Generate P-256/P-384/P-521 keys per algorithm and assert the DER signature verifies with java.security.Signature (or compare with the BC implementation output).

No test covers the new provider-selection ordering logic

detectProvider() changed from fail-fast on multiple providers to order-based selection, which is the core behavioural change of this PR (the Keycloak testsuite now has both DefaultCryptoProvider and AuthzClientCryptoProvider on the classpath). There is no unit test asserting that the higher-order provider wins, that the list is correctly sorted, or what happens when the orders are equal, so a regression in this selection (silently picking the wrong crypto provider) would go unnoticed.

Removing the multiple-provider error makes provider selection silent and non-deterministic on order ties

detectProvider() previously threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classpath. Now it just sorts by order() and takes the first, logging the rest at debug level. All three real providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider) return the same order value of 200, so if two of them ever end up on the same classpath (e.g. keycloak-crypto-default accidentally present in a FIPS deployment) the selection depends purely on ServiceLoader iteration order and the deployment silently runs with the wrong crypto stack (non-FIPS BouncyCastle instead of BCFIPS) instead of failing fast. Either keep a hard failure for equal-order providers, or give the providers distinct orders and log the ignored ones at WARN.

logger.debugf() called with a dynamically built string as the format

`logger.debugf(builder.toString())` passes a runtime-built message as the format string with no arguments. If any provider class name ever contains a '%' (or the message is changed later) the formatting throws/produces garbage inside logging. Also the message is concatenated unconditionally even when debug logging is disabled, and it ends with a dangling ", ". Use `logger.debugf("Ignored crypto providers: %s", ...)` with the joined names instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
V1 permission cleanup is now skipped when the V1 feature is disabled

Wrapping the whole listener body in `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)` means that when the V1 feature is turned off, removal of roles, clients and groups no longer disables/cleans up their V1 fine-grained permission policies. Data created while the feature was enabled (policies/resources referencing the removed role/client/group) is left behind as orphaned authorization objects, which can resurface or break if the feature is re-enabled.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission() cannot return individual clients and returns the literal "Clients" name

`getClientsWithPermission(scope)` collects resources via `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` and adds `resource.getName()` to the result set. However, the per-client resources created by `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource()` are created with `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, owner)` and never get a `type` assigned, so `findByType(..., "Clients", ...)` matches only the single resource-type resource whose name is `"Clients"`. Consequently this method (a) never returns the ids of clients that have an individual permission, and (b) returns the bogus entry `"Clients"` when an all-clients permission is granted. Callers treat the returned strings as client identifiers, so client filtering/listing based on this method is wrong in both directions.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NPE when the "Clients" resource-type resource does not exist

In `hasPermission(ClientModel, String)` the code falls back to the resource-type resource: `resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE);` and then immediately calls `authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource)`. `getResourceTypeResource()` returns `null` in several realistic cases: the realm does not have admin permissions enabled (but an admin-permissions client still exists from a previous activation), or the `Clients` resource was never created for that resource server (e.g. realms whose admin permissions client was initialized before this resource type existed). The result is a NullPointerException (HTTP 500) on every client admin REST call that evaluates a client permission instead of simply returning `false`. A null check is needed before the policy lookup (and before the subsequent `resource.getScopes()` call).

true_positives.golden_comment: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code left in new class

`ClientPermissionsV2` contains a private, never-called `getEvaluationContext(ClientModel, AccessToken)` method (it was only needed for token exchange, which now throws `UnsupportedOperationException`), an unused `logger` field (line 51), and unused imports (`Scope`, `ClientModelIdentity`/`DefaultEvaluationContext` only used by the dead method, and the static import of `AdminPermissionManagement.TOKEN_EXCHANGE`). This dead code suggests an incomplete copy from `ClientPermissions` and should be removed to avoid confusion about whether token exchange is supported here.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Client removal fails with UnsupportedOperationException when V1 and V2 fine-grained authz are both enabled

The `ClientRemovedEvent` branch calls `management(session, realm).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false)`. `management()` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2` whenever `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` is enabled, and `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` now returns `ClientPermissionsV2`, whose `setPermissionsEnabled()` throws `UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")`. Since the new guard only checks `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` (V1), a deployment with both features enabled will throw on every client deletion, failing the delete with a server error. The listener should resolve the V1 management implementation explicitly (or skip when V2 is active).

Javadoc for requireView()/requireViewClientScopes() describes a return value instead of the thrown exception

`requireView()` is documented as "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}." and `requireViewClientScopes()` as "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canViewClientScopes()} returns {@code true}." Both methods are `void` and throw `ForbiddenException` when the corresponding `can*` check fails, like the other `require*` methods documented in this file. The documentation is misleading for implementers/callers of this SPI-like interface and should state the ForbiddenException behaviour.

New schema scopes are not created for already-initialized admin permission clients

`init()` creates the authorization scopes from the schema only when the admin permissions client does not yet exist (it returns early otherwise). Adding `configure`, `map-roles-client-scope` and `map-roles-composite` to the schema therefore leaves realms whose admin-permissions client was already initialized without those scopes. In that state `getOrCreateResource()` throws `ModelException("No scopes found.")` when creating a resource for a Clients permission (line 108), and creating any client permission with the new scopes fails with a validation error from `getScope()`. A migration/upgrade step that adds missing schema scopes (and the new `Clients` resource) to existing resource servers is required.

No test coverage for the map-roles-client-scope scope and client-scope level permissions

The PR adds `MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE` to the Clients resource type and implements `canMapClientScopeRoles()`, `canManage(ClientScopeModel)`/`canView(ClientScopeModel)` and `getClientsWithPermission()` in `ClientPermissionsV2`, but the new tests only exercise `manage`, `configure`, `view`, `map-roles` and `map-roles-composite`. The scope-to-client-scope mapping path and the client-scope evaluators are therefore untested, which is where the issues above (e.g. `getClientsWithPermission` returning the resource-type name) would have been caught.

V1-only entry points now throw UnsupportedOperationException and surface as HTTP 500

`canExchangeTo()`, `isPermissionsEnabled()`, `getPermissions()` and `resource()` throw `UnsupportedOperationException`. These are still reachable while `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` is enabled: the token-exchange code path calls `clients().canExchangeTo(...)` when the V1 feature is enabled, and the admin endpoint `/admin/realms/{realm}/clients/{id}/management/permissions` calls `isPermissionsEnabled()`/`getPermissions()` unconditionally. With V2 enabled these calls now produce an uncaught runtime exception (HTTP 500) instead of a meaningful 400/404 response, and token exchange breaks outright when both features are enabled.

getResourceName() has no handling for the new Clients resource type

`getResourceName()` resolves friendly names only for the `Users` resource type ("All users" / username). For the newly added `Clients` resource type it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`, which is `null` for resources created by `getOrCreateResource()` (only name and owner are set). As a result, permissions created for clients expose a null/empty resource name through the admin API (and in the console), unlike user permissions; the name should be resolved to the client's clientId, with `"All clients"` for the resource-type resource.

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recreate exit code silently changed from 4 to 3 and 4 reused for a different meaning

`RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` is changed from `4` to `3`, and `4` is now reused for the new `FEATURE_DISABLED` result. Any existing consumer (user automation/CI pipelines built on the documented exit code, and the Keycloak Operator logic that inspects the exit code of the `update-compatibility check` run) that interprets `4` as "recreate upgrade required" will now interpret a *feature-disabled* failure as a recreate decision, and will no longer recognize a real recreate decision (`3`). This PR contains no corresponding change on the Operator/consumer side, so if the Operator hardcodes the old value the update strategy decision becomes wrong. At minimum the renumbering should be called out as a breaking change, and the Operator path that reads this code has to be verified/updated.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
CAUTION overstates that rolling-updates must be enabled for all update strategies

The new CAUTION block states that while in preview the `rolling-updates` feature "must be enabled. Otherwise, the {project_name} Operator will fail", but the NOTE immediately below describes the default (strategy not set) behaviour which mimics Keycloak 26.1 and does not require the feature — and the operator test only enables the feature for the non-default strategies. As written, users are told to enable a preview feature even when they are relying on the default behaviour. The caution should be scoped to the cases where the feature is actually required (i.e. when `spec.update.strategy` is used).

Exit code 4 description is misleading

Exit code 4 is documented as "Rolling Upgrade is not possible. The feature `rolling-updates` is disabled." In reality the command refuses to run at all and produces no compatibility verdict (see `printFeatureDisabled()`/`FEATURE_DISABLED`): no metadata is written and no comparison happens. Describing it as a rolling-upgrade verdict can lead script authors to treat it as a valid "recreate required" answer instead of a configuration error that must be fixed.

New feature-gate exit code and the renumbered recreate exit code are not asserted

`testFeatureNotEnabled` only asserts the error text and never asserts `exitCode() == 4` (`CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED`). There is also no test for `update-compatibility check` with the feature disabled, and no test asserts the new recreate exit code `3` (the `testWrongVersions` test only checks the printed message). Since the exit codes are the documented, script-facing contract of these commands (and were just renumbered in this PR), a regression in any of them would go undetected.

Test overwrites any pre-existing enabled features and only enables the flag for non-default strategies

`setEnabledFeatures(List.of(Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES.getKey()))` replaces the whole enabled-features list rather than appending, so if `getTestKeycloakDeployment()` ever sets features in the spec they are silently dropped (the preceding `getFeatureSpec() == null` guard suggests the intent was to preserve existing content). Additionally the feature is only enabled when `updateStrategy != null`, so the default (unset) strategy path runs without the `rolling-updates` feature; if the Operator is supposed to require the feature for the update logic (as the new operator docs claim), that path is untested, and if it is not required, the docs are wrong.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants manage access to admins that only have the 'view' scope on all groups

`GroupPermissionsV2.canManage()` (the no-argument variant) evaluates `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`, i.e. it returns true when the caller merely has the `view` scope on the "Groups" resource type. `canManage()`/`requireManage()` is what guards `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup`, so an admin granted only a read-only all-groups `view` permission can create top-level groups. Only `AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE` should be accepted here (the `canView()` variant above already covers view/manage). Note the new Javadoc in `GroupPermissionEvaluator#canManage()` documents this behaviour, so the doc needs fixing too, and there is no test asserting that a view-only permission cannot create/modify groups.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() returns authorization Resource IDs, not group IDs, and evaluates the wrong resource

The method iterates over authorization resources of type "Groups" and (a) calls `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)` and (b) adds `groupResource.getId()` to the returned set.

Both are wrong:
- `hasPermission(String groupId, ...)` resolves the resource via `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`. Group resources are created with the *group id as their name* (see `AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup`/`getOrCreateResource`), so passing a Resource *id* never matches; the lookup returns null and the code silently falls back to the schema-wide "Groups" resource. Per-group `view-members`/`manage-members` permissions are therefore never detected here.
- The set returned is contractually a set of *group* ids (it is fed into `session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, ...)` in `UsersResource.searchForUser`/`BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser` and into `session.users().getUsersCount(realm, ..., groupIds)`). Resource ids do not match any group, so the DB-level restriction matches no users at all.

In addition, `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` never calls `resource.setType(resourceType)` for the per-object resources it creates, so `resourceStore.findByType(server, "Groups")` only returns the single schema-wide "Groups" resource and not the individual group resources at all.

Consequence: user listing/count restricted by group membership is broken under FGAP v2 – either no users are returned for admins whose only access is `view-members` on a group (when the attribute gets set with bogus ids) or the DB query is not restricted at all. The method should use `groupResource.getName()` (the group id) for both the permission check and the returned set, and the resources must be created with the proper type.

This is copy-pasted from the method above and will mislead implementers of the interface. Similarly, `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` documents "@return Stream of IDs" while it returns a `Set<String>`.

In `hasPermission`, when no per-group resource is found the code falls back to `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE)`. That method returns `null` when the realm does not support the authorization schema (e.g. `realm.isAdminPermissionsEnabled()` is false while the admin-permissions client still exists) or when the resource is simply absent from the store. The returned value is used immediately in `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` and `resource.getScopes()` without a null check, which will throw a NullPointerException and surface as a 500 on ordinary admin endpoints (group listing, group update, user search). Add a null check and return `false`.

Removal of the global-view short circuit causes a policy evaluation per (sub)group under FGAP v2

`getSubGroups` previously hoisted `auth.groups().canView()` out of the stream and only fell back to the per-group check when the caller had no global view rights; the same change was made in `GroupsResource.getGroups`. `GroupPermissionsV2.canView(GroupModel)` does not short-circuit on an all-groups permission, so for an admin whose access comes from an all-groups `view` permission every element now triggers a `findByName` lookup plus a full policy evaluation. For groups with many children (and for group listings) this multiplies the authorization evaluations by the number of groups on the page/stream. Consider caching the all-groups decision per request as before.

getResourceName() does not resolve names for the new Groups resource type

`getResourceName` only special-cases `USERS`; for the newly added `Groups` resource type it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`. Any caller rendering permission resources (e.g. the admin console listing a scope permission's resources) will show `null`/empty instead of the group name or "All groups". A `GROUPS` branch analogous to the `USERS` one (resolving the group by id, returning "All groups" for the type resource) is needed.

The new `switch (resourceType)` dereferences `resourceType`, so a null resource type now produces a raw NullPointerException (HTTP 500) instead of the previous behaviour where `name` stayed null and the explicit `IllegalStateException("Could not map resource object with type [...]")` was thrown. `getOrCreateResource` is reachable from policy/permission creation paths; guard against null (or use the existing validation message) to keep the error actionable.

A translation that legitimately reorders two links (English `... .. ... ..`, translation with the links swapped) is reported as "Didn't find anchor tag" even though it contains exactly the same tags, i.e. a false build failure. Example: value `

x

x

`; the prefix loop yields start=3 and the suffix loop yields end=8, so `sanitized.substring(3, 8 - 8)` = `substring(3, 0)` throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. Java MessageFormat/choice syntax used in an i18next resource bundle

This bundle is consumed by the account console through i18next, where placeholders must be written as `{{0}}` (see every other entry in this file, e.g. `error-username-invalid-character='{{0}}' contains invalid character.`). The key was changed from `Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).` to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. i18next does not interpolate single braces and has no support for MessageFormat `choice`, so the user will now see the raw text including `{0}` and `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` whenever a multivalued attribute fails size validation. The surrounding `verify()` already declares `MojoExecutionException` and wraps IO errors of the main file properly, so this path produces an inconsistent, hard build failure with no actionable message. No test asserts that a valid bundle produces no findings All four tests only assert `hasItem(...)` on the returned list, so nothing verifies the absence of false positives: there is no fixture where a translation legitimately keeps the HTML of an English source that contains HTML (e.g. ``/`
`/an unchanged ``), nor a case with MessageFormat `choice` or `{{...}}` placeholders, and no assertion that `verify()` returns an empty list for such a file. Given that the new sanitizer compares the exact serialized form, a regression that starts flagging every valid bundle would not be caught by this suite. `new PropertyResourceBundle(InputStream)` is specified to decode the stream as ISO-8859-1. The theme bundles checked here (Arabic, Chinese, Greek, Ukrainian, ...) are stored as UTF-8, and the server reads them as UTF-8, so every non-ASCII value is mojibake inside the verifier. Use `new PropertyResourceBundle(new InputStreamReader(fis, StandardCharsets.UTF_8))` (same for the English bundle) to match how the files are actually encoded.

` or ``) is classified as containing no HTML. The translation is then validated with POLICY_NO_HTML and every tag it contains is reported as illegal, producing a false failure. Compile the pattern with `CASE_INSENSITIVE`.

Access token ids (`jti`, and the `token_id` event detail) change from a plain UUID to `<6-char context>:<uuid>` (e.g. `onrtac:1f65761e-...`). createRecoveryCodesCredential() serializes the full list of *raw* (unhashed) recovery codes into a JSON array and passes it as the challenge-response/value of a UserCredentialModel of type `recovery-authn-codes` to `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`. Nothing in the SPI javadoc, the UserStorage documentation, or a migration note describes it; the only example is the testsuite provider, which stores the codes in clear text and compares them with `String.equals`. Without documentation, third-party providers will either reject the update (silently falling back to local storage) or mis-store the codes. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unhealthy flusher processes are never killed (isinstance check never matches SpawnProcess)

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the kill is guarded by `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. Processes here are created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, i.e. `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`, which is *not* a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process` (that name resolves to `multiprocessing.context.Process` of the default context; `SpawnProcess` derives directly from `BaseProcess`). The guard is therefore always False in production, so `process.kill()` is never called. Previously `self.process.kill()` was invoked unconditionally. Consequence: when a flusher process is detected as hung (`cause = "hang"`), the old process keeps running while `_create_process_for_shards` starts a second process for the same shards.
