`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")` formats in the process's local timezone, while `slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` is UTC (`time.utc()`). On a deployment whose system timezone is not UTC, the two date strings can differ for the same instant, so overrides are matched to the wrong day (or not matched at all), making the whole override branch behave differently per server timezone. Use `dayjs.utc(date.start)` for the comparison.

Override end check ignores event length, allowing bookings that overrun the override

`if (slotStartTime.isAfter(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")))` only tests the slot's *start* against the override end. For an override of 14:00-15:00 and a 60-minute event, a slot starting at 14:30 ends at 15:30 but is still considered inside the override and returned as available. Since for fixed hosts in round-robin events this is the only check against that host's override window, the fixed host can be booked outside their declared override. The comparison should use `slotEndTime`.

Override timeZone is optional; dayjs .tz(undefined) silently falls back to the default timezone

Any caller of `getSlots` that passes date overrides without a `timeZone` (the field is newly added, so existing callers do not set it) will have `.tz(undefined)` resolve to dayjs's default/guessed timezone, producing a wrong `organizerUtcOffset` and shifting the override by an arbitrary amount. Either make the field required on this code path or explicitly fall back to a known timezone (e.g. UTC) when it is missing.

`startTime`/`endTime` are computed as `hour() * 60 + minute()` of the offset-shifted override time, i.e. minutes since the invitee's midnight. When the shift pushes the override across a day boundary the day information is lost: e.g. an organizer override 09:00-11:00 in UTC+5:30 viewed by an invitee in UTC-8 shifts to 19:30-21:30 of the *previous* day, but is emitted as minutes 1170-1290 of the invitee's current day, so slots are offered at a completely wrong time. Negative/over-1440 minute offsets need to be handled (clip to the day or split across days), as `buildSlots` only understands minutes within the invitee day.

The PR's primary change is that date overrides of fixed hosts are now honoured for ROUND_ROBIN events (via the new `dateOverrides`/`workingHours` handling in `checkIfIsAvailable`), but the only test added covers invitee-timezone handling for a single personal event. Consequences: (a) a reminder whose `referenceId` is still null (never handed to SendGrid) will produce a `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` with `batch_id: null`, which SendGrid rejects with a 4xx; (b) any non-EMAIL (SMS/Twilio) reminder that ever ends up with `cancelled = true` would be sent to SendGrid with a Twilio SID as batch_id. Both cases turn into request errors inside the loop, which (see the surrounding try/catch) aborts cancellation of all remaining reminders.

The `try { for (const reminder of remindersToCancel) { await client.request(...) ... } }` block wraps the entire loop in a single try/catch. If the SendGrid request for one reminder throws (invalid batch_id, rate limit, transient 5xx, auth error), the loop exits immediately, the already-queued `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` promises are never awaited, and every remaining cancelled reminder in the batch is skipped for this run. Since the cron only looks at reminders scheduled within the next hour, those skipped reminders may never be retried in time and their emails will still be delivered — exactly the failure mode this PR is meant to fix. `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` is called with `immediateDelete = true` for reminders of the original booking when a booking is rescheduled. If Twilio rejects the cancellation (e.g. the message already left the queue or the SID is no longer cancellable) the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` is skipped, so the row stays forever: the cron's cleanup `deleteMany` only targets `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`. Backup codes are stored reversibly encrypted instead of hashed

Backup codes are persisted as `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)`, i.e. recoverable plaintext for anyone with the DB dump and the shared app encryption key (the same key used for many other things and typically present in the app environment). Error/replay timestamps compared in different units, so errors are never interleaved

`gen_request_data` compares `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"]` with `event.get("timestamp", 0)`. Error timestamps come from nodestore event data, which is Unix time in **seconds**, while rrweb replay event timestamps are Unix time in **milliseconds**. Every error timestamp is therefore smaller than every replay event timestamp, so all error log lines are flushed before the first breadcrumb instead of being interleaved chronologically — defeating the purpose of this change. The unit tests hide this because the fixture segment uses second-scale timestamps (1.5, 2.0). Normalize both to the same unit (e.g. multiply error timestamps by 1000) before comparing.

Any caller that supplies `?field=...` without `error_ids` (a legal request for this endpoint signature) will get `error_ids = []` and lose all error context with no indication why. `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` returns true only when `user != null`. Before this change, `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` was executed exactly when `context.getUser() == null` (authenticate(), old else-branch) and in `challenge(context, error, field)` when the user was not yet selected. With the new helper, both call sites (lines 115 and 137) now do the opposite: the WebAuthn/conditional-UI data is only filled when a user is already set (re-authentication), and is never filled for a plain login where no user has been established yet. Consequently the normal passkeys autofill/conditional-UI on the initial username+password page disappears (no challenge, no rpId, no ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI), which breaks the primary passkeys login flow and the existing assertions in these tests that expect `//form[@id='webauth']` on the first login page. Unconditionally returning false removes the guard that skipped the passkey form for users without WebAuthn credentials

`shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators()` is overridden to always return false. `reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` only sets `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(FALSE)`, i.e. it verifies the trivial case where passkeys are disabled realm-wide. The behaviour actually changed by this PR is re-authentication with passkeys *enabled* for the realm: in that case `fillContextForm` is now invoked for an already-identified user, and because `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators()` returns false the previous 'user has no WebAuthn credential' short-circuit no longer applies. The two `try { assertThat(driver.findElement(...), nullValue()); fail(...); } catch (Exception nsee) { }` blocks (lines 291-296 and 312-317) swallow any RuntimeException from WebDriver, not just NoSuchElementException (e.g. StaleElementReferenceException or a WebDriver timeout), so the test can pass without ever proving the webauthn form is absent. true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative queryset slice is not supported by Django and will raise, not "handled automatically"

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and the client supplies a cursor with a negative offset, `start_offset = cursor.offset` is negative and `queryset[start_offset:stop]` is executed. Django QuerySets explicitly reject negative indices (`ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.`), so this path can never work: it turns a user-controlled cursor value into an unhandled 500 instead of a `BadPaginationError`/400. The inline comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually wrong. Either validate `offset >= 0` and raise `BadPaginationError`, or remove the feature.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator applies negative slice offsets to a Django QuerySet, which rejects negative slicing and raises an exception. The different exception type cited does not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`organization_context.member` can be None, raising AttributeError on every request

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated unconditionally for every GET on this endpoint, before checking `use_optimized`. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is optional and is `None` when the requester is not a member of the organization (e.g. a superuser/staff user, or an org-auth-token/API-key request that passes the `OrganizationAuditPermission` check without membership). Because Python's `or` short-circuits only when the left side is truthy, a non-superuser non-member will dereference `None.has_global_access` and the endpoint will return a 500 instead of the audit log page. Guard with `use_optimized and organization_context.member is not None` (and only compute the flag inside the optimized branch).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unguarded access to organization_context.member.has_global_access when member is None, causing an AttributeError for valid API-key or org-auth-token requests. The candidate describes a broader trigger, but the underlying bug matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key crashes for datetime sort keys

`get_item_key` applies `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly to `getattr(item, self.key)`. The only caller added in this PR (`OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`) uses `order_by="-datetime"`, so the value is a `datetime` and `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`. Every request with `?optimized_pagination=true` from an eligible user will 500 as soon as a cursor is built. Either subclass `DateTimePaginator`'s key conversion or do not use this paginator for datetime columns.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: get_item_key applies math.floor/ceil to a datetime sort key because the audit logs endpoint uses order_by="-datetime", causing a TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
"authorized administrators" gate actually grants the feature to ordinary members

The comment says the optimized path is for "authorized administrators", but the condition uses `organization_context.member.has_global_access`, which is true for any member of an organization with open membership (and for members whose role grants global access) — not just admins. Any such user can set `?optimized_pagination=true` and reach `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features=True`, which deliberately bypasses the offset lower-bound (see `paginator.py`). The access-control intent and the implemented check do not match; use an explicit admin/owner scope check if the feature is meant to be privileged, and fix the misleading comment.

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged (integer/float), but `BasePaginator.build_queryset` injects it into `WHERE "auditlogentry"."datetime" >= %s`. For the audit-log endpoint the sort key is a timestamp column, so comparing it against a bare millisecond integer either raises a database error or silently filters wrong rows. `DateTimePaginator` converts the cursor value back to a `datetime` for exactly this reason; this subclass must do the same.

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` in `BasePaginator.get_result` silently rewrites a client-supplied negative forward offset to 0, so the response no longer corresponds to the requested cursor; the next/prev cursors produced by `build_cursor` are still derived from the original (negative) `cursor.offset`, so clients can get duplicated or skipped rows instead of a clear error. Meanwhile the `is_prev` branch still passes a negative offset straight into the queryset slice, which Django rejects with `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` (500). Invalid offsets should be rejected uniformly with `BadPaginationError` rather than half-clamped.

Comment claims a behavior change that the code does not make

The added comment in `Cursor.__init__` ("Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios") describes a change, but the only code here is the pre-existing `self.offset = int(offset)`; nothing about negative offsets was enabled or validated. The comment misleads future readers into believing negative offsets are an intentionally supported/validated feature of `Cursor`, when in fact consumers such as `OffsetPaginator` still raise `BadPaginationError` for them. Remove or correct it.

The PR adds a new public paginator class with its own `get_result` implementation and a new request-controlled branch in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` (`?optimized_pagination=true`), but no tests are added for either. The paginator's datetime key handling and negative-offset path are both broken (see other findings), which a single test exercising the endpoint with the new parameter would have caught. Add tests covering: the optimized branch for an eligible user, a non-member/superuser requester (where `organization_context.member` is None), and a negative-offset cursor.

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` is a near-verbatim copy of `BasePaginator.get_result` (~60 lines) with the inline documentation about the extra before-row fetch removed. Any future fix to the base implementation (e.g. the cursor-value comparison edge case documented in the base method) will silently not apply here. Prefer overriding only the slice computation via a small hook instead of copying the whole method.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex-wide lock allows duplicate concurrent builds of the same index

Previously `BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for its whole duration, which made a concurrent `GetIndex` (RLock) block until the build finished, so a second caller observed the finished index instead of starting its own build. Now the lock is only taken around the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write, so two callers (e.g. the startup indexing goroutines in `searchSupport.init` and a watch event going through `getOrCreateIndex`) can both see `GetIndex == nil` for the same NamespacedResource and build in parallel. For file-based indexes this means two goroutines call `bleve.New(dir, ...)` on the same directory (`Root/namespace/resource.group`), and the second one fails (path already exists) or corrupts the on-disk index; for memory indexes the work is duplicated and one index is silently dropped from the cache while documents may still be written to it. The duplicate-build window needs to be guarded per key (e.g. keyed mutex / singleflight) rather than removed entirely.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race condition: narrowing cacheMu protection from the entire BuildIndex function to the final cache assignment allows multiple goroutines to build the same index for the same key concurrently.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu

`TotalDocs()` ranges over `b.cache` with no lock, while `BuildIndex` now writes to that map from many concurrent goroutines (the lock was narrowed to just the map write). Concurrent map read + write causes a fatal `concurrent map read and map write` runtime panic. This path is newly exercised on every startup by the added log line in `searchSupport.init` (`s.search.TotalDocs()`), and can also be hit at any time if metrics/logging call it while a watch event triggers a lazy index build. `TotalDocs` should take `cacheMu.RLock()`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unsynchronized iteration of b.cache in TotalDocs racing with BuildIndex writes, including the startup call in searchSupport.init and watcher-triggered index creation, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
init() goroutines write shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` without synchronization

Inside `group.Go(...)` the closures do `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...)`, both of which mutate variables declared in the enclosing function from up to `initWorkers` goroutines running in parallel. This is a data race (detectable by `-race`, and the counter reported in the `namespaces indexed` span event can be wrong/undercounted), and assigning to the shared `err` instead of returning the value through the errgroup can also overwrite an error from another worker. Use a local `err :=` inside the closure (returning it) and an atomic counter.

Stop()'s initErr is no longer surfaced; requests are served after shutdown

All the per-RPC `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil { return ... }` guards were removed, but `Stop()` still communicates shutdown exclusively by setting `s.initErr = "service is stopping"` / `"service is stopped"`. Since nothing reads `initErr` after construction anymore, calls arriving during or after shutdown no longer fail fast; they proceed against a backend whose lifecycle hooks have been stopped and whose watcher context has been cancelled, producing confusing internal errors instead of a clear "service is stopping" response. Either add an explicit closed/stopped check on the request paths or drop the now-dead initErr mutation in Stop().

Context cancel func leaked when Init fails in NewResourceServer

`ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` is created a few lines above, and on the new `s.Init(ctx)` error path the function returns `nil, err` without ever calling `cancel()`. The cancel func is also only reachable through the discarded `server` value, so the derived context (and any timer/goroutine attached to it) is leaked for the lifetime of the process. Call `cancel()` before returning the error (also applies to the `newSearchSupport` error return just above).

Index build now blocks server construction and makes startup fail hard

`NewResourceServer` now runs the full `Init` (lifecycle init + building every namespace's search index) synchronously before returning. Two consequences worth confirming: (1) process/DI startup is blocked for as long as indexing takes (the PR description says it can exceed a gRPC deadline, i.e. potentially minutes on large installs), so nothing else that depends on this constructor — including the HTTP server/readiness endpoint in single-binary mode — comes up during that time; (2) any transient failure during index build (DB hiccup, bleve directory error) now aborts construction and prevents the server from starting at all, whereas before only the failing request errored and a later request would retry `Init`. Consider doing the index build in the background with a readiness gate, or at least bounding it with a timeout and tolerating per-namespace failures.

BuildIndex still discards the span context, breaking the trace fix for builder work

The PR fixes trace propagation in `searchSupport.build` and `GetResourceStats` by assigning the derived context, but `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` still does `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)`. The builder callback invoked at line 126 uses the context captured from `searchSupport.build`, so all storage/list spans produced during the actual index build are siblings of the `BuildIndex` span rather than children, and the BuildIndex span appears empty in traces. Propagate the derived context into `builder(idx)` (e.g. by making the builder accept a ctx or by assigning `ctx, span := ...`).

Postgres integration coverage for the storage-server target is silently disabled

`TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer` now skips whenever `GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres`, leaving only MySQL exercising the storage-server module path. Given this PR changes when unified storage initializes (now inside `NewResourceServer`, i.e. during module startup), postgres is exactly the configuration where a startup regression would go unnoticed. The skip reason ("works locally") suggests the test is actually failing with these changes in CI; the root cause should be understood before merging, and the TODO should reference a tracking issue so the coverage is restored.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.

false_positives.candidate:
from_dict does no validation and silently drops the cycle-protection context

`from_dict` constructs the dataclass with `cls(**input_dict)` and returns `None` on any `TypeError`/`ValueError`. Two problems: (1) failures are silent — if the payload shape ever changes (e.g. a field is renamed or an extra key is added by a producer on a different deploy), the loop-prevention context is dropped with no log/metric and the sync cycle this PR is meant to fix reappears; (2) no type coercion is done, so after the dict round-trips through the celery broker the `queued` value comes back as an ISO string, not a `datetime`, violating the field's annotation for any future consumer that does date arithmetic on it. `sync_assignee_outbound` is an `@instrumented_task` whose signature now accepts `assignment_source_dict`, and `sync_group_assignee_outbound` always includes that key in `apply_async(kwargs=...)`. `assignment_source` added to sync_status_outbound but never used or implemented

The abstract `sync_status_outbound` now declares a 4th parameter `assignment_source`, but no caller passes it and no concrete integration implementation was updated to accept it (they rely on `**kwargs`). The result is a parameter in the published ABC signature that is dead code, misleadingly named for a status (not assignment) sync, and implies status-sync cycles are also guarded when they are not. Either wire it through the status-sync path (task + implementations) or drop it from this PR.

New `assignment_source` kwarg forwarded to all sync_assignee_outbound implementations

The task now calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)`, but no concrete integration implementation was updated in this PR. The added coverage only asserts the suppression case (`AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration)` matching the target integration blocks the outbound call). There is no test that an assignment originating from a *different* integration still produces an outbound sync, which is the main over-blocking regression risk of the new `should_sync` short-circuit, nor a test covering the celery boundary (`assignment_source_dict` serialized in `sync_group_assignee_outbound` and re-parsed in the task). false_positives.candidate:
close()/join() destroys the shared queue pool, breaking the consumer after any rebalance

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` (and `join()`, which just calls `close()`) calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which permanently stops every worker thread and calls `queue.shutdown()` on every queue. The `FixedQueuePool` is however owned by the factory (`ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` creates it once, see result_consumer.py:133) and is reused for every `create_with_partitions()` call. Arroyo closes/joins the strategy on every partition revocation/rebalance and then builds a new strategy from the same factory, so after the first rebalance the new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` is wired to a dead pool: `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`, which is swallowed by the broad `except Exception` in `submit()` (line 317-325), where the offset is then marked complete. The result is that every message after the first rebalance is silently dropped *and* its offset committed — permanent data loss plus a consumer that appears healthy while doing no work. The pool must be created/torn down per strategy instance (or close() must not shut it down).

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs in a daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is arroyo's `Commit` callback (it stages offsets on the `KafkaConsumer` and may commit them). Arroyo's `StreamProcessor`/`KafkaConsumer` offset staging is not thread-safe and expects the commit callback to be called from the thread driving `poll()`/`submit()`. Concurrent staging from this thread while the main loop polls/commits can corrupt or lose staged offsets, and if a partition has just been revoked the staged partition is no longer assigned, raising inside the loop (swallowed by `except Exception`, so commits silently stop). Offsets should be collected in the worker threads and actually committed from `poll()`/`submit()` on the main thread.

Queues are unbounded: no backpressure, unbounded memory growth

Each work queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with the default `maxsize=0`, i.e. unbounded, and `submit()` never raises `arroyo.processing.strategies.MessageRejected`. That means the strategy accepts messages as fast as Kafka delivers them regardless of how far the workers are behind, so a slow result processor leads to unbounded in-memory growth (each `WorkItem` also retains the full Kafka `Message`) and eventually OOM, plus an ever-growing `OffsetTracker.all_offsets`/`outstanding` set. The class docstring at line 253 explicitly claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", which is not true with the current configuration. Bound the queues and raise `MessageRejected` when full.

OffsetTracker state is never reset between partition assignments

The `FixedQueuePool` (and therefore its `OffsetTracker`) is created once in the factory `__init__` and shared by every `create_with_partitions()` call. On a rebalance the tracker keeps `last_committed`, `all_offsets` and `outstanding` for partitions that may no longer be assigned, and for partitions that are re-assigned it keeps a stale `last_committed`. Consequences: (a) the background commit loop will keep trying to commit offsets for partitions this consumer no longer owns, and (b) if a re-assigned partition resumes at an offset lower than the retained `last_committed`, `get_committable_offsets()` computes `start = last_committed + 1` and will never find a contiguous run, so that partition's offsets are never committed again. The tracker needs to be rebuilt (or pruned to the new assignment) in `create_with_partitions`.

shutdown() discards queued work instead of draining it

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` first sets `worker.shutdown = True` for every worker and only then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Because the workers' loop condition is checked before each `get()`, each worker finishes at most its current item and then exits, leaving all remaining queued items unprocessed and discarded — despite the docstring saying "Gracefully shutdown all workers". Additionally `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` stops the commit thread *before* calling `queue_pool.shutdown()`, and `join(timeout)` ignores its timeout argument entirely (arroyo uses it to flush in-flight work). Net effect: on every graceful shutdown/rebalance an arbitrary amount of already-consumed work is dropped and must be reprocessed after restart (duplicate processing), and the documented drain semantics of `join()` are not honoured.

A single untracked offset stalls commits for the partition forever

`get_committable_offsets()` walks offsets from `last_committed + 1` and `break`s on the first offset that is missing from `all_offsets`. There is no mechanism to ever skip a hole, so if any offset is consumed but never registered with `add_offset()`, that partition's committed offset freezes permanently and `all_offsets`/`outstanding` grow without bound. This is reachable from `submit()`: if `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` fails, the `except Exception` handler at line 317 only tracks the offset when `message.value` is a `BrokerValue`, so the offset is dropped from tracking while later offsets continue to be added. Consider tracking the offset before any decoding/validation can fail, or detecting and logging/advancing past permanent holes.

Per-message gauge emission from every worker

`metrics.gauge("remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth", ...)` is emitted in the `finally` block of every single work item, from every worker thread, with only an `identifier` tag. For a high-throughput uptime results topic this is one statsd emission per message (on top of the per-poll `total_queued` gauge), which adds measurable overhead and produces a meaningless aggregate because all N queues report into the same gauge name/tags. Emit it periodically (e.g. in `poll()`) or tag by worker id.

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts behaviour the code does not implement

The test (`assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`) asserts that a processing exception prevents the offset from being committed. The implementation does the opposite: `OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `offset_tracker.complete_offset()` in a `finally` block, so a failed item is treated as done and its offset becomes committable. The test only passes when the 1-second commit loop happens not to have ticked within the short polling window, i.e. it is an inherently racy test that will flake and that documents the wrong contract. Either change the implementation to not complete offsets for failed items (and make the test deterministic), or fix the test to assert the real at-most-once-on-error behaviour.

test_stats_reporting races against the worker threads

After submitting 10 items with a no-op `result_processor`, the test immediately asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0`. The three worker threads are already running and can drain all 10 items before the assertion executes, making this assertion flaky in CI. Either block the processor (e.g. with an event the test releases) before checking depth, or drop the `> 0` assertion.

The candidate differs in which object it describes as None, but points to the same access-control expression and failure scenario.

false_positives.candidate:
"Advanced pagination" gate is not an admin check

The comment says the feature is enabled for "authorized administrators", but the gate is `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. `request.user.is_superuser` is the raw DB flag and bypasses Sentry's required active-superuser/elevated-session check (`is_active_superuser(request)`), and `has_global_access` is true for ordinary members in open-membership organizations. No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the new endpoint query parameter

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` (including the negative-offset branch) and the new `optimized_pagination=true` branch in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` are added with no test coverage in this PR. Both are trivially broken (negative slice raises in Django, `get_item_key` cannot handle datetimes) which a single endpoint test with `?optimized_pagination=true` would have caught.

Set keys switched to sorted sets without renaming, breaking rolling deploys with WRONGTYPE

`span-buf:s:{...}` keys change type from Redis SET to ZSET (`p.zadd` here, `zcard`/`zunionstore`/`zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua, `p.zscan` in `_load_segment_data`) while keeping the exact same key names. During a rolling deploy (and for up to `redis_ttl` = 1h after it) old SET keys written by the previous version still exist; `zadd`/`zcard` against them return `WRONGTYPE`, which aborts the Lua script and raises out of `p.execute()`, crash-looping the consumer. Old pods still running will likewise get `WRONGTYPE` from `sadd`/`sscan` on the new ZSET keys. The key prefix needs a version bump (e.g. `span-buf:z:`) so the two formats cannot collide.

zunionstore uses default SUM aggregation, corrupting timestamp scores

`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call for `parent_key`) uses Redis' default `AGGREGATE SUM`. Any span payload present in both source zsets — which happens on duplicate deliveries / reprocessing of the same span — gets its score set to the sum of the two `end_timestamp_precise` values, roughly doubling it. Since the score is used as the eviction ordering key for `zpopmin`, such a span becomes effectively un-evictable while legitimate newer spans are dropped instead. Pass `AGGREGATE MIN` (or MAX) explicitly to keep scores meaningful.

Eviction limit hard-coded at 1000 while max_segment_spans config is now dead

The new eviction (`if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)`) hard-codes the segment span limit in Lua, while `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` which, after the removal of the count check in `_load_segment_data`, is no longer referenced anywhere. Operators changing `max_segment_spans` now silently get no effect, and the two values disagree (1000 vs 1001). The limit should be passed to the script as an ARGV, or the unused parameter removed.

Span eviction is now silent: no metric or log when spans are dropped

The removed block in `_load_segment_data` emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and logged when a segment exceeded the span count limit. The replacement — `zpopmin` inside add-buffer.lua — drops spans with no counter and no log, so oversized-segment truncation becomes invisible in production and silent data loss cannot be detected or quantified. The script should return the number of evicted members so the consumer can emit a metric.

The loop bound was changed from `0, 10000` to `0, 1000` and the explanatory comment ("segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. This is an unannounced behaviour change: segment trees with redirect chains deeper than 1000 will no longer be joined into a single segment, producing split segments for deep traces. If the reduction is intentional it should be documented and the retained comment updated; the PR description mentions nothing about it.

Module docstring/glossary still describes plain Redis sets

The module docstring ("Add the ingested span's payload to the set under `set_key`", and the glossary entry "span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys") is now wrong: these keys are sorted sets scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, and the scoring is what drives the new eviction behaviour. Readers relying on the docstring will not know spans are evicted lowest-timestamp-first once a segment exceeds 1000 spans.

Unguarded access to end_timestamp_precise can crash the consumer

`end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` uses direct indexing (unlike the neighbouring `val.get(...)` calls), so any message on the ingest-spans topic missing this field raises `KeyError` inside `process_batch` and kills the consumer rather than dropping/DLQ-ing the bad message. Given this is a newly required field, in-flight messages produced by older Relay versions would take the consumer down.

In the dashboard-widget split path (`get_event_stats_factory`) `_get_event_stats` is deliberately invoked with a different dataset (`discover`, `split_dataset`, etc.) while the outer `dataset` is still the metrics/transactions dataset. Substring match treats negated `!event.type:error` queries as error-focused

`_is_error_focused_query` does a raw substring test `"event.type:error" in query`. A query such as `!event.type:error` (exclude errors) or `event.type:error_foo` also contains that substring, so the function returns True. For the `discover` dataset this causes `count()` to be rewritten to `upsampled_count()` (i.e. `sum(sample_weight)`) for a query that explicitly excludes error events, producing wrong numbers for transaction/other rows (or a Snuba error because `sample_weight` is not populated for non-error rows). The check needs to parse the search query (or at least exclude negations) rather than a naive substring test.

Caching a global option behind a per-org/per-project key yields stale, inconsistent results

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches the result of `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` for 60s under a key built from `organization.id` plus a hash of the project id set. The underlying data is the *global* option `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`, which Sentry's options layer already caches in-process; writing/reading a remote cache entry per org+project-set combination adds a cache round trip per query (and the split-dataset path calls this up to 4 times per request) while providing no real speedup. Worse, when the allowlist is changed, queries keep returning the previous decision for up to 60 seconds, so the same chart can flip between upsampled (x10) and raw counts between adjacent requests - a visible data-correctness problem for a counting API. The cache key uses `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. `hash` is a 64-bit (32-bit on some builds) value with no collision guarantees, so two different project-id sets inside the same organization can map to the same key. When that happens a non-allowlisted project set will reuse the cached `True` of an allowlisted set (or vice versa), silently multiplying counts by the sample weight for projects that are not configured for upsampling. Use the actual sorted ids (or a cryptographic digest) in the key instead of `hash()`.

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called anywhere in the PR, although its docstring states it "should be called when the allowlist configuration changes to ensure cache consistency". It also cannot fulfil that promise: the cache key depends on an arbitrary project-id subset, so invalidating after an allowlist change would require enumerating every org/project-id combination that was ever queried. This leaves the misleading impression that stale cache entries are handled, when in practice they are not.

The new `SnQLFunction("upsampled_count", ...)` is registered without `private=True` (unlike the neighbouring internal functions), so any API consumer can now request `upsampled_count()` as a field/yAxis on arbitrary discover queries. The aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`, which is only meaningful for error rows in allowlisted projects; for transactions or non-upsampled errors it will either error out on the missing/unset `sample_weight` column or return meaningless values, bypassing the allowlist checks in `error_upsampling.py` entirely. Mark it private so only the internal transformation can use it.

The aggregate is wrapped in `toInt64`, and the function replaces `count()` (declared `default_result_type="integer"` elsewhere in this file), but it declares `default_result_type="number"`. The response `meta` will advertise a different field type than `count()` does, which changes client-side formatting/axis handling for the very charts this feature rewrites.

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` unconditionally returns True for `dataset == errors`, so `count()` will be rewritten to `upsampled_count() as count` for errors-dataset queries. However the function is only added to `DiscoverDatasetConfig.function_converter` in this file; the errors dataset uses its own dataset config/function converter. Unless `upsampled_count` is resolvable there, every errors-dataset timeseries query from an allowlisted project will fail with an "unknown function" validation error. No test in this PR exercises `dataset=errors`, so this path is unverified.

The unit tests only exercise the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) and the column transform. The public function added by this PR - including the cache key construction, cache hit/miss behaviour, and the interaction between a cached `False`/`True` and the dataset gate - is completely untested, which is exactly where the risky logic (stale cache, hash-based key) lives. Tests should at minimum cover a cache hit returning the stale decision and the empty-project-ids case.

`assert data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10  # First bucket has 1 event` (and the following line) claim the bucket contains 1 event while asserting 10. The 10 comes from the 0.1 client sample rate being upsampled; the comments should state that, otherwise a future reader will assume the assertion is wrong and "fix" it.

The PR adds a gitlink entry `sentry-repo` pointing at `Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a` with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. This is an accidentally committed nested checkout of the repository itself; `git submodule update --init` will fail for anyone cloning, and tooling that walks the tree (mypy `files = ["."]`, pytest collection) can behave unpredictably. It should be removed from the commit.

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` wraps both the context lookup and the `float()` conversion in bare `except Exception: pass`. If a test supplies a malformed `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` (e.g. a string, or `contexts` not being a mapping), `sample_rate` is silently not set and the test will then assert on non-upsampled counts, masking the real problem instead of failing loudly. Since this only runs in test fixtures, the errors should propagate (or at least be narrowed to `TypeError/ValueError` with an assertion).

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

A `false` value means not allowed, so `checkPermission` returns false, the code falls through to the DB (empty `fakeStore`, no permissions) and still denies. true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Ambiguous denial cache key from unescaped concatenation of name and parent

`userPermDenialCacheKey` concatenates action, resource name and parent folder with `"_"` separators. Since Grafana UIDs may contain underscores, distinct requests map to the same key: e.g. name="a_b", parent="c" and name="a", parent="b_c" both produce `<ns>.perm_<uid>_<action>_a_b_c`. A cached denial for one resource then wrongly denies a different resource the user may actually be allowed to access, for the lifetime of the entry (30s). Using a separator that cannot appear in UIDs, or hashing/length-prefixing the components, would avoid this.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify ambiguous underscore-separated concatenation in userPermDenialCacheKey, which can cause distinct requests to share a cache key and incorrectly apply cached permission denials.

Denial cache key omits identity type, allowing cross-identity collisions

The new denial cache key is built from `checkReq.Namespace.Value`, `checkReq.UserUID`, action, name and parent folder, but not from `checkReq.IdentityType`. `validateSubject` returns only the raw id portion of the subject, so different identity types can produce the same `UserUID` — e.g. `anonymous:0` and `render:0` both yield `"0"` (both forms are exercised in the tests). A denial recorded for one identity type therefore short-circuits checks for the other identity type within the same namespace, which can deny an access that should be allowed (for instance the render service, whose permissions are synthesized separately in `getRendererPermissions`, for up to the 30s TTL). Note also that the permission cache deliberately uses a distinct key per identity type (`anonymousPermCacheKey` vs `userPermCacheKey`), so the denial cache is inconsistent with it.

`Check` returns immediately on a denial cache hit (line 117) before the permission cache / DB fallback runs, and a denial is cached for every negative result (line 154, shortCacheTTL = 30s). This re-introduces exactly the staleness the PR aims to fix for the case where a Check on a given (name, folder) pair happens before the permission is granted — e.g. a probe for a dashboard/folder UID that is created immediately afterwards, or a permission grant on an existing resource. Also, for inherited access the fallback re-reads permissions but still uses the cached `folderTree` (`buildFolderTree`, 30s TTL), so a dashboard placed in a brand-new sub-folder is denied and that denial is then cached, even though fresh folder data would allow it. In `Check`, `permissionCacheUsage` is incremented with `"true"` only when the cached permissions actually allow the request, and the unconditional `"false"` increment at line 137 is reached on every cache hit that did not grant access. The metric therefore measures "allowed from cache" rather than cache hit ratio, and cache hits that end in a denial are reported as misses. Dashboards/alerts built on this metric will show a large, misleading drop in cache hit rate after this change.

GitHub user validation is skipped when the Integration row does not exist yet

The new ownership check only runs on the code path where an `Integration` row for `installation_id` already exists. When `Integration.DoesNotExist` is raised (line 481) the pipeline advances immediately and `build_integration()` resolves the installation purely with the app JWT, which does not prove the current user owns that installation. Since the `Integration` row is created asynchronously by the GitHub `installation` webhook, a user who supplies someone else's `installation_id` before the webhook is processed (or if the webhook never arrives) can still attach that installation to their own Sentry org — the exact scenario this PR intends to block. Consider validating the authenticated GitHub login against the installation account/sender fetched from `get_installation_info()` instead of relying solely on previously stored metadata.

`safe_urlopen(...)` on line 423 is outside the `try` block, and `get_user_info(...)` on line 434 calls `resp.raise_for_status()` internally. Any transport error, timeout, or non-2xx response from GitHub therefore propagates out of `dispatch()` and results in an unhandled exception/500 for the user, instead of the `error(request, self.active_organization)` page used for every other failure in this view. The GitHub authorize URL is assembled with an f-string, so `state` and especially `redirect_uri` (built from `absolute_uri`, which depends on the deployment's URL prefix) are inserted into the query string unencoded. If the URL prefix ever contains characters that must be percent-encoded (`?`, `&`, `#`, non-ASCII, a path with a query), the resulting authorize request is malformed and the OAuth step will fail or redirect somewhere unexpected. Build the query with `urlencode({...})`.

The assertion was changed from `b"The GitHub installation could not be found."` to the generic `b"Invalid installation request."`, which is the message emitted by the new OAuth/state failure branch (`error()` default), not by `build_integration()`'s `IntegrationError` for a missing installation. Combined with the hand-written `state` value (`ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`, different from every other test), the test now passes without ever reaching `get_installation_info()`, so the 404-installation path that the test is named for is no longer exercised. Either keep asserting the specific message after a valid OAuth step, or add a separate test for the state-mismatch branch.

`responses.calls[2].request.headers["Authorization"]` hard-codes the position of the app-installations request in the recorded call list, which now depends on the exact number and ordering of the new OAuth calls (`/login/oauth/access_token`, `/user`). true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing re-check of the cache after acquiring the write lock

`GetWebAssets` reads the cache under `RLock`, releases it, and then takes the write lock without re-checking whether another goroutine populated `entryPointAssetsCache` in the meantime (classic double-checked-locking recheck). Consequence: on startup, if N requests arrive concurrently with an empty cache, all N serialize on the write lock and each one re-reads and re-parses `assets-manifest.json` (or performs a CDN HTTP fetch) even though the first one already produced a valid result. In addition, every one of those late writers overwrites the already-published pointer; if a later read fails (file transiently unavailable, CDN error) the code unconditionally executes `entryPointAssetsCache = result` with `result == nil`, discarding a previously valid cached value and making subsequent callers re-do the work / receive `nil`. Adding `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` right after `Lock()`, and only assigning the cache when `err == nil`, fixes both.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the handler returns

In Create (line 51), Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163) the background goroutine builds its context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming request context. As soon as the handler returns (which happens immediately, because the goroutine is fire-and-forget), net/http cancels the request context, and every context derived from it is cancelled too. The legacy store call will therefore frequently fail with `context canceled` (or never reach the DB at all), silently losing the legacy write that mode 3 exists to keep as a safety copy. The derived context must be detached from the request, e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` before applying the timeout (while still carrying the request's auth/user values).

Create error path records a legacy-store duration for a storage failure

When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`. The failure happened in unified storage, not legacy, so the error is attributed to the wrong store and no storage-error sample is recorded at all. Any alert/dashboard on storage error rate will miss these failures while the legacy error rate shows phantom errors. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

Update error path records a legacy-store duration for a storage failure

On a failed `d.Storage.Update` the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. The failing call was against unified storage, so storage errors are never recorded and legacy error metrics are inflated with failures that did not occur in legacy. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine records a storage duration

Inside the background goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, the result is reported with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`. Legacy delete-collection latency/errors are therefore invisible, and the storage histogram is polluted with timings of legacy calls, making mode-3 metrics unusable for detecting broken legacy writes.

Fire-and-forget goroutines have no panic recovery and no lifecycle tracking

The four write paths spawn bare goroutines calling into the legacy store. (1) A panic inside a legacy store implementation (e.g. nil map/pointer in the SQL layer) is not recoverable from the goroutine and will take down the whole Grafana process, whereas in the previous synchronous code the apiserver's handler recovery would have converted it to a 500. (2) Nothing tracks in-flight goroutines, so `Destroy()` (line 172) can tear down `d.Legacy`/`d.Storage` while a goroutine is still calling into them, and in-flight legacy writes are silently dropped on shutdown. A `defer recover()` plus a WaitGroup/semaphore drained in `Destroy()` is needed.

Create passes the caller's object to the legacy store from a goroutine without deep-copying

`d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, ...)` runs concurrently with the request handler while `obj` is the very object the apiserver handler chain passed in; registry stores and legacy stores mutate the passed object (name from generateName, UID, resourceVersion, creationTimestamp). Sharing the pointer with a goroutine while the handler may still read/serialize or further mutate it is a data race (and makes the legacy row depend on timing). The object should be `obj.DeepCopyObject()`ed before handing it to the goroutine.

Legacy update now reuses the raw objInfo instead of the object written to unified storage

The previous implementation fetched the current object from storage and wrapped `objInfo` in an `updateWrapper` carrying the object actually persisted, so the legacy store received the same final state. The new code calls `d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` with the original `objInfo`, which re-runs `UpdatedObject` against the legacy store's own old object. Consequences: for PATCH/apply requests the patch is re-applied to a possibly different base, and for requests that carry a resourceVersion the value refers to the unified-storage revision, so the legacy update can fail with a conflict. Either way legacy silently diverges from unified storage (the error is only counted in a metric, not even logged). Also note `objInfo` is a request-scoped object being invoked concurrently from the goroutine, which is not guaranteed to be safe for reuse.

No test verifies that the asynchronous legacy write happens

All mode-3 tests only assert the value returned from the unified-storage mock. Because the legacy write now happens in a detached goroutine, nothing in Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection tests waits for or asserts `Legacy.*` was invoked (and `legacyStoreMock`/`storageMock` share one `mock.Mock`, so a legacy call cannot even be distinguished from a storage call). The whole point of mode 3 — that writes eventually reach legacy — is untested, so defects such as the cancelled-context issue in the goroutines cannot be caught by this suite. Use separate mocks for legacy and storage plus a channel/`assert.Eventually` to assert the legacy call.

"unified store fails" test case only configures the legacy mock

The case named "error when creating object in the unified store fails" sets up the failure via `setupLegacyFn` and leaves `setupStorageFn` nil; it only passes because `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` wrap the same `mock.Mock`, so the legacy expectation also satisfies the storage call. The test therefore does not actually exercise a unified-storage failure and would keep passing if the storage error path regressed. The same pattern appears in the List test case whose name still says "is not implemented" even though List is now implemented.
