The comment above the coldmap rules states "the default for table cells in topic list is scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%)", but the topic-list cell color was changed in this PR (`common/base/_topic-list.scss`) to `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%))`. The comment is now misleading for anyone tuning these heat/cold map colors.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The light theme color for `.topic-meta-data h5 a` was changed from `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)` to `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%)`, which may unintentionally reduce contrast and affect readability. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with design intentions.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
totalPages off by one produces an extra empty page

`totalPages` is computed as `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`. When `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit` (e.g. 150 members with limit 50) this yields 4 instead of 3. Because `showingLast` compares `currentPage` to `totalPages`, the "next" arrow stays enabled on the real last page, advancing `offset` to 150 and rendering an empty member list labelled page 4/4. Use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same pagination off-by-one: when user_count is an exact multiple of limit, the UI allows advancing to an extra empty last page (e.g. showing N/N with no members). The candidate's totalPages formula and the golden's offset capping are two descriptions of that same bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
remove_member spec uses PUT while the route only accepts DELETE

The "cannot remove members from automatic groups" example issues `xhr :put, :remove_member`, but `config/routes.rb` maps only `delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"`. Controller specs bypass verb-based route recognition, so the test passes while exercising a request that cannot actually be made against the app; a regression in the route verb would go unnoticed. Use `xhr :delete` as the other remove_member example does.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the remove_member spec issues xhr :put, but the route only maps DELETE to groups#remove_member, so the test does not exercise the actual route verb.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
totalPages off by one produces an extra empty page

`totalPages` is computed as `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`. When `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit` (e.g. 150 members with limit 50) this yields 4 instead of 3. Because `showingLast` compares `currentPage` to `totalPages`, the "next" arrow stays enabled on the real last page, advancing `offset` to 150 and rendering an empty member list labelled page 4/4. Use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same pagination bug: Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1 overcounts by one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit, producing an extra empty page. The candidate uses a different numeric example but describes the identical root cause and correct fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined
true_positives.matched_candidate:
findMembers returns undefined for unnamed groups instead of a promise

The early return was changed from `Ember.RSVP.resolve([])` to a bare `return;`, so `findMembers()` now returns `undefined` when the group has no name (the "new group" case in the admin UI). Any caller that chains on the result — e.g. `group.findMembers().then(...)`, or the controller's `next`/`previous` actions whose return value is used by the Ember action/promise machinery — will throw `TypeError: Cannot read property 'then' of undefined`. Return a resolved promise instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: a code path in findMembers lacks an explicit return, yielding undefined instead of a resolved promise for unnamed groups.

false_positives.candidate:
remove_member bypasses Group#remove, leaving user_count counter cache and primary_group stale

`group.users.delete(user_id)` on a `has_many :through` association removes the join rows with a `delete_all`, which skips ActiveRecord callbacks. `GroupUser` maintains `groups.user_count` through a counter cache / callbacks, and `Group#remove` additionally clears `users.primary_group_id` when the removed group was the user's primary group. By deleting the join rows directly, the group's `user_count` column is never decremented (so the admin group list and the new `{{user_count}}`/pagination UI show wrong totals forever) and a removed member can keep the deleted group as their primary group. The symmetric add path correctly uses `group.add(user)`; removal should use `group.remove(user)` (after looking the user up) so the same bookkeeping runs.

create silently drops alias_level

`create` only reads `params[:name]` and `params[:visible]`, but the client's `Discourse.Group#asJSON()` (used by both `create` and `save`) always sends `alias_level`, and the admin form lets you pick an alias level before the first save. As a result a newly created group is always persisted with the default alias level and the user's selection is lost without any error; it only takes effect if they save a second time (where `update` does honour `alias_level`). `create` should assign `alias_level` the same way `update` does.

Unvalidated limit/offset in public members endpoint

`limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` and `offset = params[:offset].to_i` are passed straight to `.limit()/.offset()` on this unauthenticated-reachable endpoint. A negative value (e.g. `/groups/foo/members.json?offset=-1` or `limit=-1`) makes PostgreSQL raise "OFFSET must not be negative" / "LIMIT must not be negative", turning user input into a 500, and an arbitrarily large `limit` (e.g. `limit=1000000`) forces the server to load and serialize every member of a large group, which is an easy resource-exhaustion vector. Clamp both values (e.g. offset >= 0, limit between 1 and a sane maximum).

Breaking change to /groups/:name/members.json response shape and default truncation

The endpoint previously returned a bare JSON array of serialized members (and only paginated automatic groups). It now returns `{members: [...], meta: {total, limit, offset}}` and applies a default `limit` of 50 to every group. Any existing consumer (plugins, mobile clients, scripts) that iterates the top-level array will break, and callers that relied on getting the whole membership now silently receive at most 50 users. This needs at least a changelog/version note, and ideally the pagination default should be documented; consider whether the old array shape must be preserved for compatibility.

addMembers/removeMember ignore server errors

`addMembers` and `removeMember` fire `model.addMembers(...)` / `model.removeMember(...)` without attaching a rejection handler. The server returns 422 for automatic groups and can also fail for other reasons, and unknown usernames are silently skipped by `Admin::GroupsController#add_members`. The admin therefore gets no feedback at all: the input keeps its content (see the "TODO: should clear the input"), the list is not refreshed, and nothing indicates the operation failed. Add a failure handler that surfaces the error message (as the `save` action already does).

add_members raises NoMethodError when usernames is sent as an array

`usernames.split(",")` assumes the parameter is a String. An API client (or a nested form encoding such as `usernames[]=bob`) yields an Array, and `Array#split` does not exist, producing an unhandled NoMethodError / 500 instead of a 400-class response. Coerce with `Array(params[:usernames]).join(',').split(',')` or validate the type explicitly.

Lost coverage for unknown/non-member usernames and no coverage for the new members pagination

The old specs asserted that adding a non-existent username and removing a non-member succeed silently; those cases are dropped here even though `add_members` still swallows unknown usernames, so that behaviour is now untested. Additionally, `GroupsController#members` was rewritten (new `{members:, meta:}` envelope, new default limit, new offset handling) without any spec update, so the response shape and the limit/offset edge cases are entirely uncovered.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
match_count increment is a read-modify-write race

`should_block?` loads the record, computes `record.match_count += 1` in Ruby and then saves. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked address will both read the same `match_count` and write the same value back, so matches are silently lost. Use an atomic update (e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...')` or `increment!`) instead of a full object save.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in should_block?: it performs a non-atomic match_count increment as a side effect of a read/check, creating a race where concurrent requests can lose updates. The candidate's wording is more specific but points to the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case sensitive and not normalized

`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` compares the raw value passed in by the validator against the stored string. Email local parts/domains are commonly entered with different casing (e.g. `Block@SpamFromHome.org`), and the `users.email` column is not guaranteed to be downcased at validation time, so a blocked address can be bypassed just by changing capitalization. Normalize (downcase/strip) both on write and on lookup, or compare with `lower(email)`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same case-sensitive blocked-email lookup bypass: differing capitalization can evade a stored block, and both recommend normalizing/case-insensitive comparison.

false_positives.candidate:
Validation has a DB side effect, so match statistics are double-counted

`validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, which writes to the database (increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`). Validation is not idempotent and is run multiple times per request: `UsersController#create` calls `user.valid?` (line 168) and then `user.save` (line 172), each of which runs the email validator, so a single signup attempt bumps `match_count` twice. Any other code that calls `valid?` on a user will also inflate the counters. The statistics gathering should be moved out of the validator (or made explicitly once-per-attempt).

Failed save of match statistics is silently swallowed

`record.save` is used without checking the return value. Because the model also runs presence/uniqueness validations on save, a failure (or a validation error introduced later) silently discards the `match_count`/`last_match_at` update with no log, making the statistics quietly unreliable.

Mutable array declared on the controller class is shared between instances

`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` puts a single array on the class prototype; `pushObject` in `createAccount` mutates that shared array. Any second instance of `CreateAccountController` (or the same instance reused across modal open/close) sees another instance's rejected emails, and the state is never reset. Initialize it per instance (e.g. in `init`) instead of as a class-level literal.

Server-side email error reason is replaced by generic "invalid" message

When the server rejects an email (blocked address, domain not allowed, already taken, …) the controller pushes the value into `rejectedEmails` and the validation then shows `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`. The specific reason returned in `result.errors.email` (including the new `user.email.blocked` string added to server.en.yml) is discarded, so users get a misleading "Email is invalid" message for an address that is syntactically valid. Use the server-supplied error text keyed by email instead of a generic constant.

No coverage for the whitelist/blacklist logic moved into EmailValidator

The `email_domains_whitelist` / `email_domains_blacklist` behaviour was removed from `User#email_validator` and re-implemented here (including the `elsif` precedence and the `errors[attribute].blank?` short-circuit that skips the blocked-email check). The new spec only exercises the blocked-email branch, so the relocated domain restriction code and the interaction between the two branches are untested after the refactor.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Header .panel right-alignment relies on `margin-left: auto`, unsupported by the legacy box fallbacks added in the same PR

`.panel` lost `float: right` and now relies on `margin-left: auto` plus `order: 3` to be pushed to the right of `.contents`. Auto margins for free-space distribution are a modern flexbox feature; in the legacy `-webkit-box` / `-moz-box` modes that `flexbox()` deliberately emits as fallbacks, `margin-left: auto` does not consume free space, so in those engines the header panel (user/notifications/search icons) will no longer be right-aligned — it will sit directly after the title. If those fallbacks are meant to be functional, use `-webkit-box-flex`/spacer handling or drop the legacy display values.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: removing .panel's float:right and relying on margin-left:auto/flexbox causes the header panel to lose right alignment in non-flex/legacy contexts. The candidate's legacy box fallback framing is a semantic match for the golden's non-Ember/noscript header concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() mixin maps modern `order` values directly onto 1-based legacy ordinal-group properties

`-webkit-box-ordinal-group` / `-moz-box-ordinal-group` (old 2009 flexbox spec) are 1-based and default to 1, while the modern `order` property is 0-based and defaults to 0. Emitting the same raw `$val` for both means legacy WebKit/Gecko engines see an ordering that is shifted by one relative to modern engines, and `@include order(0)` would emit the invalid `-webkit-box-ordinal-group: 0`. If the legacy prefixes are intended to work, the mixin should emit `$val + 1` for the ordinal-group properties.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: legacy -webkit/-moz box-ordinal-group properties are 1-based, so passing a 0-based order value (especially 0) produces incorrect or invalid legacy ordering. The candidate adds the appropriate fix of emitting $val + 1.

false_positives.candidate:
`float: right` on .small-action button no longer works now that .small-action is a flex container

`.small-action` was turned into a flex container (`@include flexbox()` at line 264), which makes `float` a no-op on all of its direct children. The `button { ... float: right; }` rule at line 306-310 (used for the small-action action buttons, e.g. undo/delete) will therefore no longer be pushed to the right edge; it will sit immediately after `.small-action-desc` in normal flex order. The same applies to `.topic-avatar { float: left; }` (line 270), which is now dead code. To keep the button right-aligned, use `margin-left: auto` on the button (or `flex: 1` on `.small-action-desc`) instead of a float.

align-items() mixin is inconsistent with flexbox() and will emit invalid legacy values for flex-start/flex-end/stretch

`flexbox()` emits `display: -moz-box` for legacy Gecko, but `align-items()` has no `-moz-box-align`, so legacy Gecko gets the old box display with no alignment. Additionally, `-webkit-box-align` and `-ms-flex-align` only accept the old keywords (`start`, `end`, `center`, `baseline`, `stretch`); calling `@include align-items(flex-start)` or `align-items(flex-end)` — the normal modern values — would produce invalid legacy declarations that are silently dropped, making the prefixed fallbacks useless for those values. Either translate the values inside the mixin or drop the legacy prefixes.

Percentage padding on .small-action-desc makes text indentation viewport-dependent

`.small-action-desc` changed from `padding: 0.5em 0 0.5em 4em` to `padding: 0 1.5%`. Percentage padding resolves against the containing block's width, so the horizontal inset now varies with the topic/viewport width instead of being a fixed, font-relative amount; combined with the fact that `.small-action-desc` is a flex item with no `flex` value (so it only takes its content width), the text position and wrapping of small-action messages will be inconsistent across widths. A fixed em/px padding plus `flex: 1` would be more predictable.

false_negatives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`include_website_name` is missing the trailing `?` so it is never used

ActiveModel::Serializers only consults predicate methods named `include_<attribute>?`. The method is defined as `include_website_name` (no question mark), so it is dead code and `website_name` is unconditionally serialized — e.g. it is emitted as `"website_name": null` for every user with no website, and, more importantly, it bypasses the intended guard entirely. Rename it to `include_website_name?` (and ideally base it on `website_name.present?`).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same core bug: include_website_name lacks the required trailing ? so ActiveModel::Serializers never treats it as a conditional inclusion predicate and website_name is serialized unconditionally. The candidate omits the secondary string-concatenation concern but targets the same primary issue.

false_positives.candidate:
`website_name` is not listed in `untrusted_attributes`, leaking TL0 websites to anonymous users

`:website` is declared in `untrusted_attributes` (line 109) so that a trust-level-0 user's website is hidden from anonymous visitors (anti-spam / SEO protection). The new `:website_name` attribute was added to `attributes` but not to `untrusted_attributes` and has no working inclusion guard, so the host (and now even the full path) of a TL0 user's website is serialized for anonymous requests, and `user.hbs` renders it (`{{#if model.website_name}}`). This re-exposes exactly the spam vector the untrusted_attributes list exists to block. Add `:website_name` to the `untrusted_attributes` list.

TL0/anonymous spec not updated for the new `website_name` attribute

The `untrusted_attributes` list in the 'TL0 user seen as anonymous' context still only contains `bio_raw bio_cooked bio_excerpt location website profile_background card_background`. The newly added `website_name` attribute is not asserted to be absent, which is why the regression that leaks a TL0 user's website host/path to anonymous visitors is not caught. Add `website_name` to that list (and a case asserting `website_name` is omitted when the profile website is blank).

`"" << website_host` mutates a string literal instead of concatenating

`discourse_host.ends_with?("." << website_host)` uses destructive append on the literal `"."`. It happens to work today because each evaluation allocates a fresh literal, but it will raise `FrozenError` the moment the file gets a `# frozen_string_literal: true` magic comment (or runs under `--enable-frozen-string-literal`), breaking user serialization site-wide. Use `"." + website_host` or `".#{website_host}"`.

Same-suffix heuristic treats unrelated hosts on shared domains as the same site

The second branch considers two hosts related whenever they have the same number of labels (>2) and match after dropping the first label. For shared hosting suffixes this is wrong: with an instance on `forum.github.io`, an arbitrary user website `spammer.github.io` is judged to belong to the same organisation and the full URL path is rendered instead of only the host. Since the whole purpose of showing only the host is to avoid displaying attacker-controlled path text, this heuristic should use a public-suffix check or be restricted to an exact/parent-domain match.

Only `path` is appended; query/fragment are dropped and `URI()` is re-parsed repeatedly

`website_host + URI(website.to_s).path` drops any query string or fragment, so `http://example.com/u?id=1` is displayed as `example.com/u`, which does not match the href the user clicks. It also re-parses the URI on every branch (up to twice per call) outside the `rescue nil` guard of line 138. Parse once into a local variable and build the display string from `path`, `query` and `fragment`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Kernel#open used with externally supplied URLs (SSRF / command execution)

`open(url).read` in `import_remote` and `open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` in `Jobs::PollFeed` use `Kernel#open`, which executes a shell command when the argument starts with `|` and happily fetches `file://` and internal addresses. The feed URL is a per-site setting (a site admin on a multisite install should not be able to run commands on the host), and `import_remote` is also invoked from the Disqus importer with URLs taken from the dump. Use `URI.parse(...).open`/`Net::HTTP` restricted to http(s), with a timeout.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unsafe Kernel#open call on the feed_polling_url site setting in Jobs::PollFeed, including the resulting arbitrary URL fetch/SSRF risk.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring matching

`if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }` accepts any origin that happens to be a substring of the configured Discourse URL. For `discourseUrl = "http://forum.example.com/"`, an attacker-controlled frame on `http://forum.example.co` passes the check. Compare the origin for exact equality against the parsed origin of `discourseUrl` instead, and ignore messages whose `source` is not the created iframe.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same insufficient origin validation: indexOf/substring matching can be bypassed by a malicious origin that is a substring of the configured Discourse URL. The candidate's extra source-check recommendation does not change the core issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unescaped `request.referer` interpolated into inline JavaScript (reflected XSS)

`parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')` injects the raw Referer header into a single-quoted JS string. `EmbedController#ensure_embeddable` only validates the *host* of the referer, so an attacker-controlled path/query such as `http://<embeddable_host>/x'+alert(document.cookie)+'` passes validation and breaks out of the string literal, executing arbitrary JS in the Discourse origin. Use `escape_javascript`/`j` and preferably pass only the scheme+host origin (which is all postMessage uses anyway).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly flags that postMessage should receive only the scheme+host origin rather than the full referrer URL, matching the golden issue, while also noting an additional XSS concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`<%- end if %>` is invalid Ruby and will raise a SyntaxError when the view renders

The closing tag of the if/else block is written as `<%- end if %>` instead of `<%- end %>`. The compiled template becomes `... end if <buffer append>`, i.e. the stray `if` starts a new, never-closed conditional, so rendering `embed#best` raises a SyntaxError and every embed request for an already-imported topic returns a 500. Controller specs don't render views, so this is not caught by the added tests.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the ERB closing tag uses `end if` instead of `end`, producing invalid Ruby that raises a SyntaxError when the view renders.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feed items without `content` raise NoMethodError and abort the whole poll

`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes every item exposes `content`. Many RSS 2.0 feeds only provide `description` (SimpleRSS returns nil for `content`), so `nil.scrub` raises NoMethodError. Because the items are processed in a single `each` loop with `sidekiq_options retry: false`, one such item aborts the entire polling run and all remaining items are silently skipped. Fall back to `description`/`summary` and wrap per-item processing so one bad item cannot kill the job.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: calling scrub on i.content assumes content is present, but many RSS feeds only provide description, causing a nil/NoMethodError. The candidate adds extra impact and mitigation details, but the underlying issue matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unescaped `request.referer` interpolated into inline JavaScript (reflected XSS)

`parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')` injects the raw Referer header into a single-quoted JS string. `EmbedController#ensure_embeddable` only validates the *host* of the referer, so an attacker-controlled path/query such as `http://<embeddable_host>/x'+alert(document.cookie)+'` passes validation and breaks out of the string literal, executing arbitrary JS in the Discourse origin. Use `escape_javascript`/`j` and preferably pass only the scheme+host origin (which is all postMessage uses anyway).
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same reflected/XSS-style vulnerability: request.referer is interpolated unescaped into inline JavaScript, allowing attacker-controlled referer content to break out and execute arbitrary script. The candidate adds specific code and remediation but identifies the same underlying bug.

false_positives.candidate:
raw_html cook method stores unsanitized remote HTML as `cooked`

`cook` returns `raw` verbatim for `cook_method == :raw_html`, bypassing the markdown/sanitization pipeline and the `after_post_cook` plugin filters. `Jobs::PollFeed` feeds `i.content` from an arbitrary remote RSS/Atom feed straight into `TopicEmbed.import` with this cook method, so anything the feed publisher puts in the item body (`<script>`, event handlers, iframes) is rendered verbatim to every forum visitor — a stored XSS vector. Feed/imported HTML should be run through the existing sanitizer (as `import_remote` does with its tag/attribute whitelist) before being stored as cooked.

absolutize_urls corrupts protocol-relative URLs

The check `href.start_with?('/')` also matches protocol-relative URLs like `//cdn.example.com/img.png`. Those are rewritten to `http://embedhost//cdn.example.com/img.png` (the `sub(/^\/+/, '')` strips the leading slashes), producing broken links and broken images for any feed that uses protocol-relative references. Exclude hrefs/srcs starting with `//` before prefixing.

Non-atomic SETNX + EXPIRE can permanently block retrieval of a URL

`$redis.setnx(key, "1")` followed by a separate `$redis.expire(key, 60)` is not atomic. If the process dies or the Redis connection fails between the two calls, the throttle key exists with no TTL and `retrieved_recently?` returns true forever, so that embed URL can never be imported again (the embed page will loop on the loading template indefinitely). Use `SET key 1 EX 60 NX` (or `setex` guarded by existence) instead.

This migration was already shipped; editing it to `create_table :top_topics, force: true` means that on any database where the migration is re-run (re-seeded schema, repaired schema_migrations, `db:migrate:redo`) the existing `top_topics` table is dropped along with its data instead of failing loudly. The change is also unrelated to the embedding feature in this PR and should be reverted.

The specs never render the views (controller specs don't by default), which is why the syntax error in `app/views/embed/best.html.erb` (`<%- end if %>`) goes undetected — the only new user-facing templates are completely untested. Additionally, `response.should be_success` and the X-Frame-Options assertion live in an `after` block: hook failures are reported detached from the example and run even when the example already failed, making diagnosis hard. Add a `render_views` request/controller spec for `embed#best` (both the loading and the topic-found paths).

When a `TopicEmbed` row already exists, `post = embed.post` can be nil (post hard-deleted or the association pointing at a missing row). The code then calls `PostRevisor.new(nil).revise!`, raising NoMethodError inside the retrieval job/feed poll. Guard on `post.blank?` and either recreate the topic or skip.

`contents << "\n<hr>..."` appends in place to the argument supplied by the caller rather than building a new string. `response.headers['X-Frame-Options'] = "ALLOWALL"` sets a non-standard token. Browsers that don't recognise it are entitled to fall back to denying framing, which would break embedding entirely. The reliable way to permit framing is to delete the header (`response.headers.delete('X-Frame-Options')`), optionally alongside a CSP `frame-ancestors` entry for the embeddable host.

`t.string :embed_url` creates a varchar(255). Consider `t.text` with an index on a hash/prefix, or document the limit and truncate/normalise the URL before insert.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.

In `checkIfIsAvailable`, after the date-override block, `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` returns early, before `busy.every(...)` is evaluated. This means that for any slot on a day that has a date override, existing Cal bookings and external-calendar busy times for that host are completely ignored, so already-booked slots are reported as available. Since every non-round-robin host is treated as `isFixed`, this applies to personal and collective events too, and leads to double bookings on any day with a date override. The override result must be combined with the busy check instead of short-circuiting it.

Working-hours check rejects slots when a host has multiple availability windows on the same day

The new check uses `workingHours.find((workingHour) => { ... if (start < workingHour.startTime || end > workingHour.endTime) return true; })` and treats a truthy result as "slot is outside of working hours" -> unavailable. `getUserAvailability` returns one working-hours entry per availability row, so a user with a split schedule (e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00 on the same weekday) has two entries for that day. A 10:00 slot is inside the first entry but outside the second, so `find` matches the second entry and the slot is dropped. The logic must be `!workingHours.some(entry => slot is inside entry)` (i.e. unavailable only if no entry contains the slot). As written, availability is silently broken for every user with more than one availability window per day.

Date-override check rejects slots when a host has several ranges on the same date

`dateOverrides.find((date) => { ... })` returns truthy as soon as *one* override range on the slot's date does not contain the slot, and the code then returns `false` ("slot is not within the date override"). A date override may legitimately contain multiple time ranges for the same date (e.g. 09:00-11:00 and 14:00-16:00). A slot inside the first range is outside the second, so it is incorrectly marked unavailable. The predicate must be inverted to "no range on that date contains the slot".

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")` formats in the process's local timezone, while `slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` is UTC (`time.utc()`). On a deployment whose system timezone is not UTC, the two date strings can differ for the same instant, so overrides are matched to the wrong day (or not matched at all), making the whole override branch behave differently per server timezone. Use `dayjs.utc(date.start)` for the comparison.

Override end check ignores event length, allowing bookings that overrun the override

`if (slotStartTime.isAfter(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")))` only tests the slot's *start* against the override end. For an override of 14:00-15:00 and a 60-minute event, a slot starting at 14:30 ends at 15:30 but is still considered inside the override and returned as available. Since for fixed hosts in round-robin events this is the only check against that host's override window, the fixed host can be booked outside their declared override. The comparison should use `slotEndTime`.

Override timeZone is optional; dayjs .tz(undefined) silently falls back to the default timezone

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` is called with `override.timeZone` typed as optional (`timeZone?: string` in packages/types/schedule.d.ts). Either make the field required on this code path or explicitly fall back to a known timezone (e.g. UTC) when it is missing.

`startTime`/`endTime` are computed as `hour() * 60 + minute()` of the offset-shifted override time, i.e. minutes since the invitee's midnight. When the shift pushes the override across a day boundary the day information is lost: e.g. an organizer override 09:00-11:00 in UTC+5:30 viewed by an invitee in UTC-8 shifts to 19:30-21:30 of the *previous* day, but is emitted as minutes 1170-1290 of the invitee's current day, so slots are offered at a completely wrong time. Negative/over-1440 minute offsets need to be handled (clip to the day or split across days), as `buildSlots` only understands minutes within the invitee day.

The PR's primary change is that date overrides of fixed hosts are now honoured for ROUND_ROBIN events (via the new `dateOverrides`/`workingHours` handling in `checkIfIsAvailable`), but the only test added covers invitee-timezone handling for a single personal event. There is no test with a round-robin event type where a fixed host has a date override and the round-robin host does not, which is exactly the regression-prone path (and the path where the `dateOverrideExist -> return true` short-circuit and the split-working-hours bug manifest). Please add a getSchedule test for that scenario, including a host with multiple availability windows on the override day.

The matcher iterates with `.every()` over the *actual* slots and compares them index-wise to `expectedSlots`, without comparing array lengths. If the implementation returns fewer slots than expected (e.g. the first N are correct but trailing slots are dropped), the assertion still passes. The newly added timezone assertion relies on this matcher, so a partial regression in override handling would go unnoticed; the matcher should also assert `schedule.slots[dateString].length === expectedSlots.length`.

Non-atomic retryCount update can lose increments

`retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` computes the new value from the value read earlier in the request. If two cron invocations overlap (or the job is retried while a previous run is still processing), both read the same value and write the same result, losing an increment and allowing more retries than intended. Use Prisma's atomic update `{ retryCount: { increment: 1 } }` instead. Same issue at line 195.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race condition: computing retryCount from a previously read value can lose increments under concurrent runs, and recommends Prisma's atomic increment. It also notes the same issue in the other update location.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteMany retryCount clause is not scoped to SMS reminders

The new `OR` branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` in the `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany` call has no `method` filter, so this SMS-only cron will delete *any* WorkflowReminder row (EMAIL, WHATSAPP, mandatory reminders, etc.) whose retryCount exceeds 1, including rows that were already successfully scheduled. Any future code path that increments retryCount for a non-SMS method will silently have its reminders purged by this endpoint. The branch should be combined with `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` (and ideally `scheduled: false`).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in scheduleSMSReminders.ts: the deleteMany OR clause filters only on retryCount > 1 without restricting method to SMS, so it can delete non-SMS workflow reminders. The candidate's suggested fix matches the golden concern.

false_positives.candidate:
retryCount is never incremented when sendTo/message is missing, so reminders are retried forever

The retryCount increment only happens inside the `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)` block (else branch) or in the `catch`. When `sendTo` is null/empty (e.g. a booking with no `smsReminderNumber`, which is one of the main failure modes this PR targets) or the rendered message is empty, the loop silently does nothing: the reminder stays `scheduled: false` with retryCount 0 and will be re-processed on every cron run until the scheduled date passes. The same applies to the `continue` at line 69 when `workflowStep`/`booking` is missing. These cases should also bump retryCount (or delete the reminder).

Prisma update inside catch block can throw and abort the whole cron run

The `prisma.workflowReminder.update` added at the top of the `catch` block is itself unawaited-by-try: if it rejects (e.g. the reminder row was deleted concurrently → Prisma P2025 record-not-found), the rejection escapes the catch, aborts the remaining reminders in the loop and returns a 500 instead of the intended per-reminder error handling. Wrap it in its own try/catch (or use `updateMany`, which does not throw on no match).

retryCount filter in deleteMany has no supporting index

The new `retryCount` column is used in a `deleteMany` predicate (`retryCount > 1`) that runs on every cron invocation, but no index covers it and the existing indexes (`[method, scheduled, scheduledDate]`, `[cancelled, scheduledDate]`) do not help because the predicate is an unscoped OR branch. On a large WorkflowReminder table this forces a sequential scan each run. Scoping the branch to method/scheduled (so an existing index can be used) or adding an index would avoid the repeated full-table scan.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unreachable branches in getBaseConditions

`getAuthorizationConditions()` always resolves to a `Prisma.Sql` instance (never null/undefined — it returns `NOTHING_CONDITION` on failure), so `authConditions` is always truthy and the `else if (filterConditions)` / final `else { return NOTHING_CONDITION; }` branches at lines 76-80 can never execute. This dead code hides the fact that the "no authorization" case is already represented by `1=0`; it should be simplified to avoid future readers assuming a null-auth path exists.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same dead-code issue in getBaseConditions: getAuthorizationConditions always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql, so authConditions is always truthy and the later else-if/else branches are unreachable.

false_positives.candidate:
getBaseConditions() can return an un-parenthesized OR expression

`getBaseConditions()` returns the raw SQL fragment as-is when there are no filters, and for `org`/`team` scope that fragment is `(A AND B) OR (C AND D)` with no surrounding parentheses (see the reducers at lines 171-174 and 204-207). Any caller that composes it, e.g. `WHERE ${baseConditions} AND "startTime" > $x`, gets `(A AND B) OR ((C AND D) AND "startTime" > $x)` because `AND` binds tighter than `OR`. The first OR branch then bypasses the extra predicate entirely, which silently returns rows that should have been filtered out (a correctness and potential data-exposure problem, since the OR branches are the authorization clauses). The fragment returned by `getBaseConditions()` (and by `getAuthorizationConditions()`/`getFilterConditions()`, which are public) should always be wrapped in parentheses, e.g. `return Prisma.sql`(${conditions})``.

Public findMany() removed without updating consumers

The public method `findMany(findManyArgs: Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedFindManyArgs)` is deleted and replaced by `getBaseConditions()`, which only returns a SQL fragment and performs no query. Any existing caller of `InsightsBookingService.findMany` (tRPC insights routers, etc.) will fail to compile/run, and no such callers are updated in this PR (only the service and its test are touched). Either keep a `findMany`-equivalent that executes the query using the new SQL conditions, or update all call sites in the same change.

Constructor options type widened, losing discriminated-union safety

The constructor parameter type was changed from the discriminated union `InsightsBookingServiceOptions` to the new flat `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` (`scope: "user" | "org" | "team"`, `teamId?: number`). With this signature, `{ scope: "team", userId, orgId }` (no `teamId`) type-checks, then fails `safeParse`, sets `this.options = null`, and silently yields `1=0` — i.e. insights pages render empty data instead of surfacing a compile-time or runtime error. Keep the discriminated union as the public input type, or throw when validation fails so misuse is visible.

SQL expectations depend on unordered DB row order

The org-scope and team-scope assertions compare the generated `Prisma.Sql` (including its bound `values`) against literal arrays such as `[testData.user.id, user2.id, user3.id]` and `[testData.org.id, testData.team.id, team2.id, team3.id]`. Those arrays come from `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds` / `TeamRepository.findAllByParentId`, which are issued without an `ORDER BY`, so Postgres may return rows in any order and the test will fail intermittently. Sort the actual/expected ID arrays before comparing, or assert on membership rather than exact array ordering.

Caching tests deleted without replacement

The `describe("Caching")` block covering `cachedAuthConditions`/`cachedFilterConditions` memoization was removed entirely. The caching behaviour still exists in the service (lines 84-95 of insightsBooking.ts) and is now untested, so a regression (e.g. the `=== undefined` check for the nullable filter cache) would go unnoticed. The tests could have been ported to the new `Prisma.sql` expectations like the others.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token", destroying valid stored refresh tokens

When the provider response has no `refresh_token`, the function sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. This runs on the normal (non credential-sharing) path too. For providers whose schema makes `refresh_token` optional — e.g. `packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`, where the result is spread with `{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }` and persisted — the real, still-valid refresh token in the DB is overwritten with the useless string `"refresh_token"`, so the next refresh fails and the user must reconnect. Only inject a placeholder when it is actually needed, or leave the field absent so the spread keeps the existing token.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string 'refresh_token', invalidating the stored token and breaking subsequent refreshes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
minimumTokenResponseSchema computed keys are nonsense and strip every token field except access_token

`[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the string `"[object Object]"` (Zod types have no `toString` override), so the object literal ends up with a single extra key literally named `"[object Object]"`, with the second definition overwriting the first. The resulting schema is effectively `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown }`. Because `z.object` strips unknown keys by default, when credential sharing is enabled the parsed data loses `expires_in`/`expiry_date`/`refresh_token`/`scope`/etc. Callers that spread `tokenResponse.data` into the stored credential (e.g. office365calendar) will therefore persist a credential with no expiry and a bogus refresh token. The intent ("allow any extra properties, require access_token plus a numeric expiry") needs `.passthrough()` / `z.record()`, not computed keys.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in minimumTokenResponseSchema: computed keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] are invalid Zod usage. The candidate elaborates on the resulting key collision and field stripping, but the underlying issue matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Google credential key is overwritten with the zod SafeParse wrapper object

`parseRefreshTokenResponse()` returns the result of `schema.safeParse(...)` (i.e. `{ success: true, data: {...} }`), not the parsed object, but the return value is assigned to `key` and written straight into `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. Previously the code used `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` which returned the credential object itself. As a result, after the first token refresh the stored Google Calendar credential becomes `{"success":true,"data":{...}}`, which no longer satisfies `googleCredentialSchema` on the next load, permanently breaking Google Calendar for that user. It should store `...data` (and ideally only after checking `success`).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse wrapper, but that wrapper is persisted as the credential key instead of the parsed token payload, breaking subsequent loads. The candidate also proposes storing the parsed data after checking success.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Credential-sync path returns a fetch Response where callers expect an axios/SDK/gaxios response

When credential sharing is enabled the helper returns a raw `fetch` `Response`, but the call sites consume very different shapes: `zoho-bigin` and `zohocrm` read `tokenInfo.data.error` / `tokenInfo.data.access_token` (axios response), `hubspot` assigns the return value to a `HubspotToken` and reads `expiresIn`/`accessToken` (SDK object), and `googlecalendar` reads `res?.data` (gaxios response). A `Response` has none of these properties, so with `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` configured these refresh paths throw `TypeError` or silently store `undefined` tokens. The helper needs to normalise the sync response per call site (or each call site must handle both shapes).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: the credential-sync helper returns a raw fetch Response, while callers such as Google Calendar and HubSpot expect integration-specific token/response shapes, causing runtime failures unless the return value or call sites are normalized.

true_positives.golden_comment: When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

Credential-sync path returns a fetch Response where callers expect an axios/SDK/gaxios response

When credential sharing is enabled the helper returns a raw `fetch` `Response`, but the call sites consume very different shapes: `zoho-bigin` and `zohocrm` read `tokenInfo.data.error` / `tokenInfo.data.access_token` (axios response), `hubspot` assigns the return value to a `HubspotToken` and reads `expiresIn`/`accessToken` (SDK object), and `googlecalendar` reads `res?.data` (gaxios response). A `Response` has none of these properties, so with `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` configured these refresh paths throw `TypeError` or silently store `undefined` tokens. The helper needs to normalise the sync response per call site (or each call site must handle both shapes).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify that the sync endpoint returns a raw fetch Response whose shape is incompatible with callers expecting .data or token object fields, causing runtime errors or undefined tokens.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
zoho-bigin passes credentialId where refreshOAuthTokens expects userId

`refreshOAuthTokens(fn, "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` — the third parameter of `refreshOAuthTokens` is the Cal.com `userId`, which is sent to the external sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. Passing the credential's id means that, with credential sharing enabled, the self-hosted endpoint is queried for the wrong user, so either the request fails or (worse) another user's tokens are fetched and stored on this credential. `refreshAccessToken` should receive and forward `credential.userId`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: refreshOAuthTokens is invoked with credentialId where it expects the Cal.com userId, causing incorrect user lookups and credential sync failures. The candidate adds implementation details but points to the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Refresh success is checked via `response.statusText !== "OK"`

`statusText` is not guaranteed to be populated (HTTP/2 and several fetch implementations return an empty string for a 200 response), so this check can throw `HttpError` with an empty message on a perfectly successful token refresh, and it also treats any non-200 2xx as success. Use `response.ok` / `response.status` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug in the Salesforce OAuth token refresh flow: success is incorrectly determined from response.statusText rather than response.ok/status, which can misclassify successful responses and cause authentication failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Salesforce connection is built with the stale access token after refreshing

`getClient` fetches a new access token and stores it in the DB, but then constructs `new jsforce.Connection({ ..., accessToken: credentialKey.access_token })` using the *old* token from the credential instead of `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token` (and `instanceUrl: credentialKey.instance_url` instead of the refreshed `instance_url`). The refresh is therefore pointless: all subsequent API calls still use the expired token and will fail with 401/INVALID_SESSION_ID.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that the jsforce connection is created with stale credential values after token refresh, causing subsequent API calls to use stale credentials.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unvalidated request body and decryption failures produce unhandled 500s; no HTTP method guard

`appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a `ZodError` on a malformed payload, and `symmetricDecrypt(...)` / `JSON.parse(...)` throw on a bad key or non-JSON plaintext. None of these are caught, so the handler returns an unhandled 500 (with a stack trace in the logs/response depending on config) instead of a 400 with a useful message. There is also no method check, so a `GET`/`DELETE` to this route reaches the body parse and 500s. Use `safeParse` + explicit 400s and restrict the handler to POST.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that schema.parse throws on invalid payloads and yields an unhandled 500 instead of a controlled 400 response. The candidate adds related decryption/JSON and method-guard concerns, but the core bug matches.

false_positives.candidate:
`prisma` is used but never imported in Salesforce CalendarService

`await prisma.credential.update(...)` was added to `getClient`, but there is no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` in the file (the import list only adds `zod` and `parseRefreshTokenResponse`). This is a compile error under type-check and a `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` at runtime, which means every Salesforce CalendarService instantiation (i.e. every booking/availability call involving Salesforce) will throw.

Salesforce refreshes the token and writes the credential on every service instantiation

The new refresh_token request and `prisma.credential.update` run unconditionally inside `getClient`, which is called from the constructor. There is no expiry check (unlike every other app, which only refreshes when the stored token is expired). Every Salesforce CalendarService creation — including availability lookups — now issues a token request to `login.salesforce.com` plus a DB write, which wastes requests, risks hitting Salesforce's OAuth rate limits, and adds latency to the booking path. Gate the refresh on the stored expiry.

Zoom sends appSlug "zoomvideo" while the app's slug is "zoom"

`refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoomvideo", credential.userId)` sends `appSlug=zoomvideo` to the credential sync endpoint, but the Zoom app's slug everywhere else in the codebase (and in the `App` table / the new `/api/webhook/app-credential` lookup) is `zoom` — see `zoomvideo/api/callback.ts` which creates the credential with `appId: "zoom"`. The self-hoster therefore receives an identifier that does not match the slug it must post back, so Zoom credential syncing cannot work without a special case.

Credential sync request carries no authentication and its status is never checked

The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` with no shared secret/signature (contrast with the inbound webhook, which requires `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`). The remote endpoint therefore cannot distinguish a request from Cal.com from any other caller, so an endpoint implemented as documented hands out user access tokens to anyone who can reach it. The response status is also never checked, so an error page/HTML body is passed on to the caller as if it were a token response. A signed header (or reuse of `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`) and an `response.ok` check are needed, and the expected request/response contract should be documented.

Synced credential update does not clear the `invalid` flag

When a credential already exists the handler only updates `key`. Credentials that were previously marked `invalid: true` (e.g. by `invalidateCredential` in the Zoom/Webex adapters, or the `invalid_grant` path in Google Calendar) stay flagged after fresh working keys are pushed in, so Cal.com keeps treating the app as broken and shows the "reconnect" state even though the parent application has supplied valid tokens. The update should also set `invalid: false`.

Webhook secret compared with `!==` (non constant-time) and header lookup is case-sensitive

The shared secret check uses a plain string comparison, which is vulnerable to timing analysis; use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. Additionally, `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME]` relies on the operator configuring a lowercase header name (Node lowercases incoming header keys); if they configure `Calcom-Webhook-Secret` every request silently 403s. Lowercase the configured name before the lookup instead of only documenting the requirement in `.env.example`.

No tests for the new credential-sync webhook or token parsing helper

This PR adds a new unauthenticated-by-default HTTP surface that writes OAuth credentials into the database (`/api/webhook/app-credential`) plus two shared helpers (`parseRefreshTokenResponse`, `refreshOAuthTokens`) that are now on the refresh path of ~10 apps, and ships with no unit/integration tests (the PR description confirms this). Given that the helpers change the stored credential shape for Google, Office365, Salesforce and others, regressions here silently break every user's calendar/video integrations. At minimum, tests covering secret rejection, create vs update behaviour, and the enabled/disabled branches of the two helpers should be added.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Workflow reminder cancellation promises are not awaited before the handler returns

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are async but are invoked inside `forEach` without `await` and are no longer accompanied by awaited prisma promises (the `remindersToDelete` array that used to be awaited was removed). The handler can return (and in a serverless environment the function instance can be frozen/terminated) before the `workflowReminder.update({ cancelled: true })` / `delete` writes are issued, leaving the reminder un-cancelled so the reminder email/SMS is still sent. Collect the promises and `await Promise.all(...)` before returning.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are async but invoked inside forEach without await, so reminder cancellation may not complete and scheduled reminders can remain active. The candidate's serverless/handler framing is a specific consequence of the same missing-await issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path cancels the SendGrid send but never removes the WorkflowReminder row

When `immediateDelete` is true the function issues the SendGrid cancel request and returns early, without deleting the `workflowReminder` row or setting `cancelled = true`. Callers no longer delete the row themselves (the previous `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany` calls were removed from handleCancelBooking/bookings.tsx/handleNewBooking). For the reschedule path in handleNewBooking the row therefore stays in the DB with `scheduled: true` and a live `referenceId` until the cron's `deleteMany` for past `scheduledDate` eventually removes it, and if the SendGrid call fails there is no record that the cancellation is still pending (no retry by the cron, since `cancelled` is not set). Either delete the row or mark it cancelled on this path.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the immediateDelete=true path cancels the SendGrid email but returns without deleting or marking the WorkflowReminder record cancelled, leaving an orphaned DB row inconsistent with the other path. Minor wording differences about the SendGrid call do not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
remindersToCancel query is not filtered by method/scheduled/referenceId

The query that collects reminders to cancel only filters on `cancelled: true` and `scheduledDate`. It does not filter `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`, `scheduled: true`, or `referenceId: { not: null }`. Consequences: (a) a reminder whose `referenceId` is still null (never handed to SendGrid) will produce a `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` with `batch_id: null`, which SendGrid rejects with a 4xx; (b) any non-EMAIL (SMS/Twilio) reminder that ever ends up with `cancelled = true` would be sent to SendGrid with a Twilio SID as batch_id. Both cases turn into request errors inside the loop, which (see the surrounding try/catch) aborts cancellation of all remaining reminders.

One failed SendGrid cancellation aborts cancellation of all remaining reminders

The `try { for (const reminder of remindersToCancel) { await client.request(...) ... } }` block wraps the entire loop in a single try/catch. If the SendGrid request for one reminder throws (invalid batch_id, rate limit, transient 5xx, auth error), the loop exits immediately, the already-queued `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` promises are never awaited, and every remaining cancelled reminder in the batch is skipped for this run. Since the cron only looks at reminders scheduled within the next hour, those skipped reminders may never be retried in time and their emails will still be delivered — exactly the failure mode this PR is meant to fix. The try/catch should be per-reminder inside the loop.

SendGrid API key is never set on the @sendgrid/client singleton used for cancellation

This module only calls `sgMail.setApiKey(sendgridAPIKey)`. `@sendgrid/mail` holds its own internal `Client` instance, while the default export of `@sendgrid/client` imported here as `client` is a separate singleton whose API key is never set (contrast `emailReminderManager.ts`, which calls both `sgMail.setApiKey` and `client.setApiKey`). As a result every `client.request(...)` in this file — including the new cancellation calls — is sent unauthenticated and fails with 401; the error is swallowed by the catch, so cancellations silently never happen and the reminder emails are still sent. Add `client.setApiKey(sendgridAPIKey)`.

Reschedule path still cancels SendGrid sends immediately, re-exposing the 100 pending-cancellation limit

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` is called with `immediateDelete = true` for reminders of the original booking when a booking is rescheduled. That issues the `scheduled_sends` cancel straight away, and each cancellation occupies a slot in SendGrid's pending-cancellation list until the scheduled send date — which is the exact quota (max 100 pending cancellations) the PR description identifies as the root cause of reminders still being delivered. Rescheduled bookings (one of the two cases named in the PR title/issue) therefore still hit the original failure, while cancelled bookings go through the new deferred path. This should use the deferred `cancelled` flag like the cancellation path.

WorkflowReminder row is leaked when Twilio cancellation throws

`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` awaits `twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId)` before deleting the DB row, and the whole body is wrapped in a try/catch that only logs. If Twilio rejects the cancellation (e.g. the message already left the queue or the SID is no longer cancellable) the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` is skipped, so the row stays forever: the cron's cleanup `deleteMany` only targets `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`. Previously the caller deleted the row independently of the Twilio result. Delete the row even when the provider call fails.

Unused `Prisma` import and non-prettier-formatted import list

`Prisma` was moved into the value import but all of its uses (`PrismaPromise<Prisma.BatchPayload>`) were removed in this diff, so the binding is now unused, and it is added without a trailing comma, which violates the repo's prettier config. Both will fail the lint/format checks in CI.

try/catch no longer protects the now-async forEach callback

The callback passed to `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach` was made `async`, so the enclosing `try { ... } catch (error) { logger.error(...) }` can never catch anything thrown inside it: rejections from `await getCalendar(...)` or `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` escape as unhandled promise rejections instead of being logged, and `Reschedule` returns `true` and sends the reschedule email before the calendar/video events are actually cancelled. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (ref) => ...))` inside the try block.

getCalendarCredentials now returns pending promises in its `calendar` field

`getCalendarCredentials` is still synchronous but `getCalendar(credential)` now returns `Promise<Calendar | null>`, so each returned item's `calendar` property is a promise rather than a `Calendar`. This silently changes the public shape of `ReturnType<typeof getCalendarCredentials>` for every consumer (only `getConnectedCalendars` was updated here); any other caller that uses `item.calendar` directly will get a promise object at runtime. Additionally the promises are created without handlers, so if a CalendarService constructor/import rejects for a credential that is never awaited, the rejection goes unhandled. Consider making the function `async` and resolving the calendars (e.g. with `Promise.all`) before returning, so the contract stays `Calendar | null`.
